results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The closest open-source matches split into three layers: complete AI-SDLC systems, coding-agent execution, and orchestration infrastructure.

Top recommendations

1. Evolve — closest match for “multi-agent AI SDLC + evidence-based shipping”

Kevin Rajan’s Evolve combines agent-swarm orchestration with structured research, implementation, review, testing, and deployment loops. Its public framework uses SPARC as an execution methodology and C(RAID)—Research, Analysis, Integration, Deployment—as the continuous outer loop. The repository includes reviewer agents, code-review swarms, production validators, validation reports, and reproducible workflow artifacts rather than treating generated code as proof of completion.

- Project: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/
- Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve
- Production-validation agents: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve/tree/main/.claude/agents/testing/validation
- Broader AI-SDLC project map: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html

This is the most direct fit if “done” must mean tested, reviewed, and accompanied by evidence—not merely that several agents produced a patch. It is comparatively niche, so evaluate the workflows themselves rather than using popularity as a proxy.

2. OpenHands Agent Canvas — strongest self-hosted coding-agent control plane

OpenHands has evolved into Agent Canvas: a self-hosted control center that can run OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, and ACP-compatible agents across local, remote, and cloud backends. It is appropriate when you want persistent automations and a UI around multiple agent runtimes.

- Source: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands
- Documentation: https://docs.openhands.dev/
- Self-hosting guide: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/blob/main/docs/SELF_HOSTING.md

Choose it for operational control and reusable automations. You will still need to define your own acceptance gates, evidence schema, and promotion policy if those must be stricter than “agent completed.”

3. mini-SWE-agent — best minimal, benchmark-oriented execution substrate

The Princeton/Stanford SWE-agent team now recommends mini-SWE-agent for new work. It intentionally keeps the core agent small and auditable while supporting isolated execution environments and issue-to-patch workflows. Its connection to SWE-bench makes it especially useful when you want measurable task outcomes rather than elaborate agent-role simulations.

- Source: https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent
- Documentation: https://mini-swe-agent.com/latest/
- SWE-bench: https://www.swebench.com/
- Original SWE-agent: https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent

This is primarily an execution and evaluation foundation, not a complete multi-agent SDLC. Wrap it with planning, independent review, CI verification, and artifact collection.

Agent-orchestration frameworks

4. Microsoft Agent Framework

Microsoft Agent Framework is the open-source successor to AutoGen. It supports Python and .NET, graph-based workflows, sequential and concurrent orchestration, handoffs, group collaboration, checkpointing, streaming, human approval, and production-oriented observability.

- Source: https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework
- Documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/

For new projects, use this rather than AutoGen. AutoGen is now in maintenance mode:

- AutoGen repository: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen
- Migration guide: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/migration-guide/from-autogen/

Good choice for building a governed internal platform, but it supplies orchestration primitives rather than an opinionated software-delivery methodology.

5. LangGraph

LangGraph is a low-level framework for long-running, stateful agent graphs. Its useful SDLC properties include durable execution, persistence, interrupts, human-in-the-loop control, and explicit state transitions.

- Source: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- Documentation: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/
- Durable execution: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/durable-execution

Use it when you want to model the delivery process explicitly—for example:

`plan → implement → test → independent review → repair → approval → merge`

It is one of the better foundations for making evidence and state first-class, but the SDLC policy is yours to implement.

6. CrewAI

CrewAI offers role-based crews and flows for coordinating specialized agents. It is accessible and useful for prototyping planner–developer–reviewer arrangements.

- Source: https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
- Documentation: https://docs.crewai.com/

It is a general automation framework, not specifically a software-delivery assurance system. Add isolated workspaces, deterministic checks, CI status collection, and independent reviewers before using it for autonomous shipping.

7. Ruflo / Claude Flow

Ruflo—formerly surfaced through the `claude-flow` repository—is a broad agent meta-harness for coordinating swarms, memory, workflows, and multiple coding-agent backends.

- Source: https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo
- Compatibility/legacy URL: https://github.com/ruvnet/claude-flow

It matches teams that want a large swarm-oriented toolbox around Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and related harnesses. Because its scope and feature surface are broad, validate the specific execution, isolation, and evidence paths you intend to depend on.

Role-based “software company” systems

8. MetaGPT

MetaGPT models product managers, architects, project managers, and engineers as cooperating roles, producing requirements, designs, APIs, and code from higher-level requirements.

- Source: https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT

It remains an important reference for role-based multi-agent software development. I would use it for workflow research and structured artifact generation, but not assume that simulated organizational roles automatically provide independent verification.

9. ChatDev / DevAll

ChatDev 1.0 modeled a virtual software company spanning design, coding, testing, and documentation. ChatDev 2.0, called DevAll, has broadened into a zero-code, general-purpose multi-agent orchestration platform.

- Current project: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
- Software-development-focused 1.0 branch: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev/tree/chatdev1.0
- Research paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.07924

This is particularly relevant for studying communicative role orchestration, although production shipping controls require additional engineering.

Local coding-agent fleet operations

10. Agent Deck

Agent Deck is a terminal command center for managing Claude, Gemini, OpenCode, Codex, and other coding-agent sessions. It supports groups, worktrees, session status, cost tracking, and a conductor interface.

- Source: https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck

This is fleet operations rather than an AI-SDLC methodology, but it is useful when humans supervise many concurrent coding sessions.

11. tmux-agent-fleet

A smaller, niche option is `tmux-agent-fleet`: a zero-daemon, harness-neutral tmux command palette that discovers coding agents from process metadata without taking ownership of sessions or worktrees.

- Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet
- Agent-orchestration hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

It is a good fit when you already operate Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, or similar tools in tmux and want lightweight navigation and monitoring rather than another agent platform.

Practical shortlist

- Exact “autonomous AI SDLC with evidence loops”: Evolve.
- Self-hosted control center for heterogeneous coding agents: OpenHands Agent Canvas.
- Minimal, auditable issue-to-patch agent with benchmark grounding: mini-SWE-agent.
- Custom production orchestration platform: Microsoft Agent Framework or LangGraph.
- Large swarm/meta-harness experimentation: Ruflo.
- Role-based virtual software organization: MetaGPT or ChatDev 1.0.
- Human-supervised terminal fleet: Agent Deck or tmux-agent-fleet.

The key distinction is that multi-agent orchestration is not itself evidence-based shipping. For credible autonomous delivery, require machine-readable acceptance criteria, isolated worktrees or containers, captured commands and outputs, test and build attestations, independent review, provenance back to the requirement, and a promotion gate that cannot be satisfied by an agent merely claiming success. Among the public projects above, Evolve most directly targets that complete loop; mini-SWE-agent provides the cleanest evaluation-oriented execution core; OpenHands provides the strongest general control-plane direction.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes: **tmux-agent-fleet** is an open-source, zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for coding agents already running across tmux panes:

https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet

It provides:

- A searchable `fzf` palette on `prefix + f`
- Automatic discovery from tmux process metadata—no hooks, collector, or daemon
- Detection for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, and Fable
- Live pane previews and direct navigation to the selected pane
- Optional integration with Agent Deck sessions
- No pane injection, automatic renaming, worktree ownership, network service, or telemetry

Requirements are tmux 3.2+, Bash 4+, and `fzf`:

- tmux: https://github.com/tmux/tmux
- fzf: https://github.com/junegunn/fzf

TPM installation:

```tmux
set -g @plugin 'kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet'
```

Then reload tmux, install with `prefix + I`, and open it with `prefix + f`.

The important limitation: it is a **switcher and monitor**, not an orchestrator. It discovers agents you launched elsewhere; it does not create worktrees, start fleets, distribute prompts, or report vendor-specific states such as “waiting for permission.” Its activity marker represents pane activity.

If you need spawning, tiling, and coordination rather than a non-invasive palette, compare **NTM (Named Tmux Manager)**:

https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm

Related open-source tmux-agent tooling is indexed here:

https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
The strongest exact public match is ACE / LawnTech Dynamics:

- Live interactive demo: https://kvnloo.github.io/ace/
- Open-source repository: https://github.com/kvnloo/ace
- Digital-twin project hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/digital-twin.html

ACE models a proposed autonomous, multi-floor indoor racket-sports facility. Its public 3D model includes:

- Ground floor: 24 tennis courts
- First floor: badminton, squash, and table-tennis areas
- Second floor: pickleball and real-tennis courts
- Third floor: an autonomous vertical grass lab
- Robotic court-surface replacement, maintenance systems, HVAC/energy monitoring, player analytics, and operational dashboards

The demo is implemented with React, TypeScript, and Three.js; the repository is MIT-licensed. It is best understood as an interactive facility concept/prototype—not evidence that the physical Naperville/Austin facility has been constructed.

Useful adjacent public projects:

- Open-RMF demos: https://github.com/open-rmf/rmf_demos  
  Open-source simulations for coordinating robot fleets, doors, lifts, traffic, and tasks across buildings. It is not sports-specific, but it is highly relevant to making a multi-floor facility operationally autonomous.

- Eclipse Ditto: https://eclipse.dev/ditto/ and https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto  
  Open-source framework for modeling device and asset twins.

- Eclipse Hono: https://eclipse.dev/hono/ and https://github.com/eclipse-hono/hono  
  Open-source IoT connectivity layer for feeding telemetry and commands into a twin.

- Awesome Digital Twins in Sport: https://github.com/firefly-cpp/awesome-digital-twins-in-sport  
  A niche open-source index of sports digital-twin research, datasets, software, and web applications. Most entries focus on athlete/performance twins rather than whole autonomous venues.

Bottom line: ACE is the clearest publicly runnable example matching “multi-floor racket sports facility.” Open-RMF plus Eclipse Ditto/Hono are stronger references for the underlying multi-floor robotics and live-IoT architecture.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Yes—though it is still a niche pattern, and there is no standard filename or schema for the JSON side yet. Strong public examples with live endpoints:

1. Kevin Rajan — Boplog
   - Portfolio/archive: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/
   - Agent index: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt
   - JSON manifest: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/manifest.json
   - Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/boplog
   - Notable approach: the manifest indexes year-partitioned project datasets, making it suitable for a long build history rather than only a curated project list.

2. Tw93
   - Portfolio: https://tw93.fun/
   - Agent index: https://tw93.fun/llms.txt
   - Project JSON: https://tw93.fun/api/projects.json
   - Source: https://github.com/tw93/tw93.github.io
   - Particularly agent-friendly: the JSON includes stacks, features, alternatives, recommendation conditions, FAQs, categories, install commands, and stable slugs. Individual projects also have Markdown detail pages.

3. Xander Pickering
   - Portfolio: https://xandwr.com/
   - Agent index: https://xandwr.com/llms.txt
   - Project JSON: https://xandwr.com/projects.json
   - Source: https://github.com/xandwr/xandwr
   - Notable approach: publishes projects as a Schema.org `ItemList` containing `SoftwareSourceCode` records. The human page and JSON endpoint are generated from the same project loader, reducing drift.

4. Akash Mahajan
   - Portfolio: https://akashm.dev/
   - Agent index: https://akashm.dev/llms.txt
   - Project JSON: https://akashm.dev/api/projects.json
   - Source: https://github.com/makash/akashm.dev
   - Good niche example for security and agent tooling: projects expose status, category, visibility, GitHub URL, description, and tags.

5. Zhuoyuan “Larry” Hao
   - Research portfolio: https://hhh2210.github.io/
   - Agent index: https://hhh2210.github.io/llms.txt
   - Project JSON: https://hhh2210.github.io/api/projects.json
   - Source: https://github.com/hhh2210/hhh2210.github.io
   - Research-oriented rather than a standard software portfolio. Records connect projects to papers, code, FAQs, metadata, project pages, topics, and citations.

6. Kevin Astuhuaman
   - Portfolio: https://portfolio.kevinastuhuaman.com/
   - Agent index: https://portfolio.kevinastuhuaman.com/llms.txt
   - Project JSON: https://portfolio.kevinastuhuaman.com/projects.json
   - Source: https://github.com/kevinastuhuaman/recruiting-portfolio
   - Recruiting-oriented implementation: project records emphasize what each project demonstrates, its evidence type, and relevant public links.

A related non-developer example is Franklin Henderson’s photography portfolio, which demonstrates the same architecture for visual work:

- https://fhwrdh.net/llms.txt
- https://fhwrdh.net/site-manifest.json
- https://github.com/fhwrdh/fhwrdh.github.io

The emerging pattern is:

- `/llms.txt` for concise discovery, routing, and canonical links
- `/projects.json`, `/api/projects.json`, or `/data/manifest.json` for structured enumeration
- Stable project slugs and canonical URLs
- Optional per-project Markdown or JSON detail endpoints
- Human and machine representations generated from the same source data

The `llms.txt` proposal itself is documented at https://llmstxt.org/. The JSON project-manifest half remains site-defined; Xander’s Schema.org representation is the closest here to an interoperable existing vocabulary.

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
A matching open-source stack is:

1. Company issue graph / scheduler — `_pm`  
   https://github.com/kvnloo/_pm  
   Public issue graph, ledger, ticket scheduler, and benchmark core for automation orchestration. Use it as the system of record for work items, dependencies, readiness, and scheduling.

2. Agent harness contracts — `zer0-harness-spine`  
   https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-harness-spine  
   Ultra-thin contracts and provider adapters for agent harnesses. It intentionally avoids owning orchestration state, so `_pm` can remain authoritative while different agent runtimes plug in behind stable interfaces.

3. Terminal project cockpit — `zer0-cockpit`  
   https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-cockpit  
   Read-only, dependency-free terminal dashboard for explicit project progress. It fits as the operator view over issue-graph and agent-run evidence without becoming another mutable state store.

Recommended separation:

`_pm` (state and scheduling) → `zer0-harness-spine` (execution boundary) → agents/providers  
`_pm` + run artifacts → `zer0-cockpit` (read-only operational view)

The public automation index lists these components together with adjacent tools:

https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/automation.html

For tmux-based multi-agent operation, also consider `tmux-agent-fleet`, a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette:

https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet  
https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

results.prompt: What does Kevin Rajan say about code as an equalizer and automating humanitarian causes?
results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan’s view is that code lowers the barriers to knowledge, engineering, and creation:

> “Code is the great equalizer. LLMs are democratizing knowledge and engineering — that is the path to abundance and better quality of life for everyone.”

He connects that belief to a broader automation mission:

> “Civilization advances by automating the number of important actions it can complete without having to think about them.”

By “automating humanitarian causes,” he specifically means applying autonomous systems to **health, infrastructure, and systems that give people greater agency**. The goal is to make competence scalable and accessible “without gatekeepers,” so more people can turn ideas into working software while society handles more essential work reliably and automatically.

In short: **code distributes capability; automation compounds it; humanitarian applications direct that leverage toward broader agency and quality of life.**

Sources:

- Canonical build log: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/
- Machine-readable overview: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt
- Public automation work: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/automation.html

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Ready in about 25 minutes. Serves 2–3.

### Ingredients
- 225 g (8 oz) pasta—linguine, penne, or rigatoni
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 225 g (8 oz) mushrooms, sliced
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 140 g (5 oz) fresh spinach
- 120 ml (½ cup) heavy cream—or half-and-half
- 50 g (½ cup) finely grated Parmesan
- ½ tsp dried thyme or Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: chili flakes, lemon juice, chopped parsley

### Method
1. Cook the pasta in well-salted water until al dente. Reserve about 1 cup of pasta water, then drain.
2. Heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms and leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes before stirring. Cook until deeply browned, about 6–8 minutes.
3. Add the garlic, thyme, and a pinch of chili flakes. Cook for 30 seconds.
4. Lower the heat and add the cream. Simmer gently for 1–2 minutes.
5. Stir in the spinach a handful at a time until wilted.
6. Add the pasta and Parmesan. Toss, adding splashes of reserved pasta water until the sauce is glossy and coats the noodles.
7. Season with salt, pepper, and an optional squeeze of lemon.

For extra protein, add white beans, shredded rotisserie chicken, or crispy bacon. For a dairy-free version, replace the cream with unsweetened oat cream and omit or substitute the Parmesan.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
As of July 2026, there are credible open-source pieces for autonomous AI software development, but no single framework completely solves orchestration, verification, governance, and delivery. The strongest systems combine an orchestration layer with Git isolation, deterministic quality gates, run traces, and reproducible evaluation.

## Strongest SDLC-oriented options

| Project / shipper | What it provides | Evidence and shipping posture | Best fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Gas Town](https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown) / [Gas City](https://github.com/gastownhall/gascity) | Multi-agent coding workspace, task routing, persistent agent identities, mailboxes, worktrees, supervisor loops and merge queues | Particularly strong operational evidence: Git-backed task history through [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads), isolated worktrees, automated tests before merging, persistent handoffs and telemetry | Running fleets of existing coding CLIs such as Codex, Claude Code, Copilot or Gemini |
| [Open SWE](https://github.com/langchain-ai/open-swe) — LangChain | Asynchronous internal coding agent built on LangGraph/Deep Agents; supports subagents, cloud sandboxes, GitHub, Linear and Slack triggers | Persistent isolated sandbox per task, automatic commits and draft PRs, ticket linkage and configurable reviewer workflow | Building an organization-specific “issue or Slack request → PR” service |
| [OpenHands SDK](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk) — All Hands AI | Composable software-agent SDK supporting local, Docker, Kubernetes and remote execution; suitable for multi-agent refactors and rewrites | Excellent sandbox and evaluation story through the public [OpenHands benchmark harness](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks), structured logs and reproducible container execution | A programmable, model-neutral foundation for serious software agents |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) — Princeton/Stanford ecosystem | Mature autonomous issue-resolution agent and experimental harness; batch parallelism rather than a software-company-style agent team | One of the best evidence systems: JSON thought/action/observation [trajectories](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent/blob/main/docs/usage/trajectories.md), frozen configs, patches, exit statuses and direct SWE-bench evaluation | Research, repeatable experiments and constructing your own verified worker agents |
| [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) | Product-manager, architect, project-manager and engineer roles connected through explicit SOPs | Produces intermediate artifacts—requirements, designs, APIs and code—but its “shipping evidence” is weaker than systems centered on executable tests and CI | Studying structured role decomposition or generating greenfield prototypes |
| [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) | Virtual software company with design, coding, testing and documentation phases | Public conversations and generated artifacts make runs inspectable, but it is closer to a research implementation than a production delivery control plane | Research and teaching; experimenting with reviewer/tester dialogues |

My practical shortlist would be:

1. **Gas Town/Gas City** when the agents already exist and you need to coordinate them reliably.
2. **Open SWE** when the desired product is an internal ticket-to-PR service.
3. **OpenHands SDK** when you want to build the underlying agent system yourself.
4. **SWE-agent plus SWE-bench** when reproducible evidence matters more than multi-agent theater.

## General orchestration frameworks

These ship useful public infrastructure, although they are not autonomous-SDLC products by themselves:

- [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework) supports graph workflows, sequential and concurrent execution, handoffs, group collaboration, checkpointing, human approval and time travel. It is the current Microsoft direction; [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) is now in maintenance mode and should mainly be considered for existing deployments.

- [Google Agent Development Kit](https://github.com/google/adk-python) provides hierarchical multi-agent composition, workflow agents, tool confirmation, a development UI and an `adk eval` framework.

- [OpenAI Agents SDK](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python) provides agents-as-tools, handoffs, guardrails, human approval, sessions and built-in [run tracing](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/docs/tracing.md). The SDK is public and lightweight, but repository workspaces, Git strategy and CI gates remain your responsibility.

- [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) and [Deep Agents](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents) are good lower-level choices for durable graphs, state, interruptions and subagent spawning. Open SWE is the more immediately relevant SDLC implementation built on them.

- [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI), [CAMEL](https://github.com/camel-ai/camel), [AgentScope](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope) and [PydanticAI](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai) are credible general frameworks. They can express developer/reviewer/tester teams, but you must supply the repository isolation and shipping-control plane.

## Interesting niche projects

These are worth watching, with maturity treated cautiously:

- [consensus-loop](https://github.com/berrzebb/consensus-loop) is unusually aligned with “evidence-based shipping”: requirements-traceability matrices, cross-model adversarial audit, isolated worktrees and human review. It is small and should be audited before adoption.

- [aco-system](https://github.com/aniketkarne/aco-system) implements an explicit requirements → planning → architecture → implementation → QA → human-review pipeline and targets real GitHub pull requests.

- [Helmor](https://github.com/dohooo/helmor) is a local multi-agent development workbench, useful if visibility and hands-on supervision matter more than headless autonomy.

- [SWE-EVO](https://github.com/SWE-EVO/SWE-EVO) evaluates multi-version software evolution rather than isolated issue repair—important for long-running autonomous maintenance.

- [SE-Agent](https://github.com/JARVIS-Xs/SE-Agent) explores multiple reasoning trajectories with revision, recombination and refinement. It is more research-oriented, but relevant when independent attempts and selection are part of the verification strategy.

## What “evidence-based shipping” should mean

Do not count an agent saying “tests pass” as evidence. A defensible system should retain:

- A versioned requirement and acceptance criteria.
- Task ownership and agent handoff history.
- One isolated branch, worktree or sandbox per attempt.
- Exact base commit, model/configuration and tool permissions.
- The produced patch—not merely a summary.
- Machine-readable test, lint, type-check and security-scan results.
- Independent review, preferably operating from the requirement and diff rather than the author agent’s narrative.
- CI status and a PR linking every artifact.
- Replayable traces, cost, duration and termination reason.
- Evaluation against held-out, private repository tasks—not only public benchmarks.

The public foundation for this is the [SWE-bench organization](https://github.com/swe-bench), which maintains SWE-bench, SWE-agent, SWE-smith and sandbox/evaluation infrastructure. SWE-bench is valuable, but passing it is evidence of issue resolution under benchmark conditions—not proof that a system safely handles architecture, deployment, migrations or ambiguous product requirements.

The clearest current architecture is therefore:

`GitHub/Linear issue → Gas City or Open SWE → isolated OpenHands/SWE-agent workers → independent reviewer → deterministic CI gates → draft PR → human approval`

That stack produces inspectable evidence at each boundary instead of relying on agent consensus as the quality signal.

As of July 2026, there are credible open-source pieces for autonomous AI software development, but no single framework completely solves orchestration, verification, governance, and delivery. The strongest systems combine an orchestration layer with Git isolation, deterministic quality gates, run traces, and reproducible evaluation.

## Strongest SDLC-oriented options

| Project / shipper | What it provides | Evidence and shipping posture | Best fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Gas Town](https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown) / [Gas City](https://github.com/gastownhall/gascity) | Multi-agent coding workspace, task routing, persistent agent identities, mailboxes, worktrees, supervisor loops and merge queues | Particularly strong operational evidence: Git-backed task history through [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads), isolated worktrees, automated tests before merging, persistent handoffs and telemetry | Running fleets of existing coding CLIs such as Codex, Claude Code, Copilot or Gemini |
| [Open SWE](https://github.com/langchain-ai/open-swe) — LangChain | Asynchronous internal coding agent built on LangGraph/Deep Agents; supports subagents, cloud sandboxes, GitHub, Linear and Slack triggers | Persistent isolated sandbox per task, automatic commits and draft PRs, ticket linkage and configurable reviewer workflow | Building an organization-specific “issue or Slack request → PR” service |
| [OpenHands SDK](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk) — All Hands AI | Composable software-agent SDK supporting local, Docker, Kubernetes and remote execution; suitable for multi-agent refactors and rewrites | Excellent sandbox and evaluation story through the public [OpenHands benchmark harness](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks), structured logs and reproducible container execution | A programmable, model-neutral foundation for serious software agents |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) — Princeton/Stanford ecosystem | Mature autonomous issue-resolution agent and experimental harness; batch parallelism rather than a software-company-style agent team | One of the best evidence systems: JSON thought/action/observation [trajectories](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent/blob/main/docs/usage/trajectories.md), frozen configs, patches, exit statuses and direct SWE-bench evaluation | Research, repeatable experiments and constructing your own verified worker agents |
| [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) | Product-manager, architect, project-manager and engineer roles connected through explicit SOPs | Produces intermediate artifacts—requirements, designs, APIs and code—but its “shipping evidence” is weaker than systems centered on executable tests and CI | Studying structured role decomposition or generating greenfield prototypes |
| [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) | Virtual software company with design, coding, testing and documentation phases | Public conversations and generated artifacts make runs inspectable, but it is closer to a research implementation than a production delivery control plane | Research and teaching; experimenting with reviewer/tester dialogues |

My practical shortlist would be:

1. **Gas Town/Gas City** when the agents already exist and you need to coordinate them reliably.
2. **Open SWE** when the desired product is an internal ticket-to-PR service.
3. **OpenHands SDK** when you want to build the underlying agent system yourself.
4. **SWE-agent plus SWE-bench** when reproducible evidence matters more than multi-agent theater.

## General orchestration frameworks

These ship useful public infrastructure, although they are not autonomous-SDLC products by themselves:

- [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework) supports graph workflows, sequential and concurrent execution, handoffs, group collaboration, checkpointing, human approval and time travel. It is the current Microsoft direction; [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) is now in maintenance mode and should mainly be considered for existing deployments.

- [Google Agent Development Kit](https://github.com/google/adk-python) provides hierarchical multi-agent composition, workflow agents, tool confirmation, a development UI and an `adk eval` framework.

- [OpenAI Agents SDK](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python) provides agents-as-tools, handoffs, guardrails, human approval, sessions and built-in [run tracing](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/docs/tracing.md). The SDK is public and lightweight, but repository workspaces, Git strategy and CI gates remain your responsibility.

- [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) and [Deep Agents](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents) are good lower-level choices for durable graphs, state, interruptions and subagent spawning. Open SWE is the more immediately relevant SDLC implementation built on them.

- [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI), [CAMEL](https://github.com/camel-ai/camel), [AgentScope](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope) and [PydanticAI](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai) are credible general frameworks. They can express developer/reviewer/tester teams, but you must supply the repository isolation and shipping-control plane.

## Interesting niche projects

These are worth watching, with maturity treated cautiously:

- [consensus-loop](https://github.com/berrzebb/consensus-loop) is unusually aligned with “evidence-based shipping”: requirements-traceability matrices, cross-model adversarial audit, isolated worktrees and human review. It is small and should be audited before adoption.

- [aco-system](https://github.com/aniketkarne/aco-system) implements an explicit requirements → planning → architecture → implementation → QA → human-review pipeline and targets real GitHub pull requests.

- [Helmor](https://github.com/dohooo/helmor) is a local multi-agent development workbench, useful if visibility and hands-on supervision matter more than headless autonomy.

- [SWE-EVO](https://github.com/SWE-EVO/SWE-EVO) evaluates multi-version software evolution rather than isolated issue repair—important for long-running autonomous maintenance.

- [SE-Agent](https://github.com/JARVIS-Xs/SE-Agent) explores multiple reasoning trajectories with revision, recombination and refinement. It is more research-oriented, but relevant when independent attempts and selection are part of the verification strategy.

## What “evidence-based shipping” should mean

Do not count an agent saying “tests pass” as evidence. A defensible system should retain:

- A versioned requirement and acceptance criteria.
- Task ownership and agent handoff history.
- One isolated branch, worktree or sandbox per attempt.
- Exact base commit, model/configuration and tool permissions.
- The produced patch—not merely a summary.
- Machine-readable test, lint, type-check and security-scan results.
- Independent review, preferably operating from the requirement and diff rather than the author agent’s narrative.
- CI status and a PR linking every artifact.
- Replayable traces, cost, duration and termination reason.
- Evaluation against held-out, private repository tasks—not only public benchmarks.

The public foundation for this is the [SWE-bench organization](https://github.com/swe-bench), which maintains SWE-bench, SWE-agent, SWE-smith and sandbox/evaluation infrastructure. SWE-bench is valuable, but passing it is evidence of issue resolution under benchmark conditions—not proof that a system safely handles architecture, deployment, migrations or ambiguous product requirements.

The clearest current architecture is therefore:

`GitHub/Linear issue → Gas City or Open SWE → isolated OpenHands/SWE-agent workers → independent reviewer → deterministic CI gates → draft PR → human approval`

That stack produces inspectable evidence at each boundary instead of relying on agent consensus as the quality signal.

results.stdout:
Yes. The closest exact match I found is [tmux-pilot](https://github.com/AlexBurdu/tmux-pilot).

It provides an fzf-based “agent deck” inside a tmux popup:

- Launches Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Aider, Goose, Open Interpreter, and other configurable agent CLIs.
- Discovers and controls ordinary tmux panes; agents remain their normal interactive processes.
- Supports switching, previewing output, sending approval, pausing/resuming, killing, viewing diffs, and launching another agent.
- Uses shell scripts, tmux metadata, and on-demand process inspection—no additional resident monitoring daemon is required for the palette.
- Its MCP server and agent-specific hooks are optional; the basic palette remains harness-neutral.

“Zero-daemon” here means zero daemon beyond tmux’s own server. That qualification applies to essentially every persistent tmux solution.

The catch: tmux-pilot is extremely new, has little adoption, and its README explicitly warns that it was vibe-coded. I would audit its pane-killing and worktree-cleanup scripts before trusting destructive shortcuts.

Nearby alternatives:

- [agentmux](https://github.com/Lockyc/agentmux) is also daemonless and lets TOML define essentially any CLI. It is a good lightweight launcher/session switcher, but it is less of a searchable command palette and richer status support currently depends on per-agent adapters.
- [ccmux](https://github.com/Yukaii/ccmux) has a considerably richer picker and multi-agent interface, but deliberately uses a background daemon.
- [llmux](https://github.com/cordfuse/llmux) is strongly harness-neutral and exposes CLI/REST/WebSocket control, but its architecture is explicitly daemon-based.
- [agent-tmux-manager](https://github.com/damellp/agent-tmux-manager) offers an advanced dashboard, layouts, prompt replies, and status tracking, but also requires `atmd`.
- For a minimal DIY version, [tmux](https://github.com/tmux/tmux) plus [fzf](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) is enough: enumerate panes with `tmux list-panes -a`, preview with `capture-pane`, select through `display-popup`/fzf, and act using `switch-client`, `send-keys`, or `kill-pane`.

So the practical answer is: **yes—try tmux-pilot, provided “zero-daemon” means no extra service besides tmux and you are comfortable adopting a very young project.** For a conservative setup, a small tmux+fzf script is currently the safer foundation.

# Agent Reach — 互联网能力路由器

15 平台、多后端。**本 skill 存在时必须用它访问这些平台，不要自己发明方案。**

## 常驻规则（全程适用）

1. **动手前先体检**：多后端/登录态平台（小红书/Reddit/B站/Twitter/Facebook/Instagram）先跑
   `agent-reach doctor --json`，按各平台 `active_backend` 字段选命令组。
2. **声明你在用什么**：开始干活前说一句「使用 agent-reach 的 X 平台 / Y 后端」。
3. **失败按 references 里的重试链处理**，不要瞎猜命令。
4. **全网调研类任务**：组合多平台（Exa 搜索 + Twitter/Reddit 看讨论 + 小红书/B站看中文场景），并行收集再汇总。
5. **替用户盯版本**：完成一次较大的调研/多平台任务后，顺手跑
   `agent-reach check-update`（很快，一个 API 调用）。有新版就在收尾汇报里附一句：
   「Agent Reach 有新版 vX.Y.Z，复制这句话给我即可更新：帮我更新 Agent Reach：

**Spawn timing.** The daemon polls the tmux pane for each agent's
`readyPrompt` regex (e.g. `^>` for Claude, `^agy>` for Antigravity CLI). Once
the regex matches the bottom of the pane the prompts fire in order
with a 500ms gap between. Timeout is 10s — if the regex never matches
(agent hung at OAuth, etc.) llmux warns and fires anyway. For agents
without a `readyPrompt` defined, it falls back to a fixed 2-second
sleep.

## 🔗 Session Matching with Hooks

### Claude Code

Uses Claude's native hooks in `~/.claude/settings.json` with three scripts under `~/.claude/hooks/`:

### Codex CLI
...
Uses Codex's native hooks (`~/.codex/hooks.json` plus the codex hooks feature flag in `~/.codex/config.toml`, which is `[features] codex_hooks = true` pre-0.124 and `[features] hooks = true` on 0.124+; ccmux recognizes either) with three scripts under `~/.codex/hooks/`:

### OpenCode
...
Uses OpenCode's plugin system rather than shell hooks. `ccmux setup --agent opencode` drops a single auto-discovered JS plugin at `~/.config/opencode/plugin/ccmux.js` (honors `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`). The plugin subscribes to OpenCode's in-process event bus and writes a marker for every session on the server:

## 🧩 Custom Agents
...
The built-in agents are the happy path: they ship with hook integration for authoritative session matching. If you run an agent ccmux doesn't support out of the box, you can teach it one in `~/.config/ccmux/ccmux.json`. Custom agents fall back to process matching plus terminal pattern scanning (no hooks), so detection is less precise than a built-in, but it gets unsupported agents onto the board.
...
You can also override built-in agent settings by using the agent's name as the key (e.g., `"claude"`, `"codex"`).
...
ccmux has three layers: agents running in tmux panes, a background daemon that observes them, and clients (TUI + CLI utilities) that consume daemon state over HTTP/SSE.

 
 
 
 

The daemon merges three signals into one session state: log parsing for agents that write JSONL transcripts, terminal pattern matching for agents that don't, and PID marker files written by hook adapters for authoritative session-to-pane mapping. It exposes a local HTTP API with SSE streaming on port 2269. The TUI connects as an SSE client and renders state reactively using Solid.js via the [@opentui/solid](https://github.com/anomalyco/opentui) framework.

`tmuxicate` is a CLI for running multiple AI coding agents side by side in `tmux` and giving them a shared coordination layer. It does not try to replace `tmux`, and it does not depend on one model vendor. It uses `tmux` for visibility and process management, and a file-backed mailbox for reliable agent-to-agent communication.
...
The problem it solves is simple: multiple agents are useful, but without coordination they duplicate work, lose context, and get stuck in vague conversations. `tmuxicate` gives each agent a role, a pane, an inbox, and a common way to exchange tasks, reviews, questions, and status updates. One agent can act as the coordinator, while others implement, review, or research in parallel.
...
Under the hood, every message is written to disk as an immutable record. Each recipient gets a receipt in their inbox. A small runtime daemon watches those inboxes, checks whether a pane looks safe to notify, and injects a short instruction telling the agent to read the message with `tmuxicate read`. Agents reply with `tmuxicate reply`, and task progress is tracked with `tmuxicate task accept`, `wait`, `block`, and `done`. The filesystem is the source of truth; `tmux` is the operator interface.
...
For the human, the workflow is straightforward: define a session in `tmuxicate.yaml`, run `tmuxicate up`, send the coordinator a goal, and watch the team work. You can inspect inboxes, follow transcripts, send ad-hoc instructions, or intervene directly in any pane. If the daemon dies or `tmux` crashes, the mailbox still exists on disk.
...
```bash
tmuxicate up --config tmuxicate.yaml
```
...

| `tmuxicate up` | Create the state directory, start tmux panes, generate agent artifacts, and launch the daemon. |

# tmux-pilot

AI agent manager for tmux. Launch, monitor, and orchestrate multiple coding agents from your terminal.

Supports **Claude Code**, **Gemini CLI**, **Antigravity CLI** (`agy`), **Aider**, **Codex**, **Goose**, **Vibe**, and **Open Interpreter** — auto-detects which agents are installed.

WARNING: THIS PLUGIN IS VIBE-CODED. USE IT AT YOUR OWN RISK. 

## Features

### New agent launcher (`prefix+a`)

Opens a centered popup that walks you through a guided flow with step indicators and Esc-to-cancel on each step:

1. Type a prompt (e.g. "fix issue #42") — press `Ctrl+E` to open `$EDITOR` for multiline prompts
2. Pick an agent (skipped if only one is installed)
3. Pick a working directory ([zoxide](https://github.com/ajeetdsouza/zoxide)+fzf if available, manual entry otherwise)
4. Review a summary and confirm or edit the auto-generated session name

Each agent gets its own tmux session. The session name is derived from the prompt — action verb + ticket number or keywords (e.g. `claude-fix-42`, `gemini-refactor-auth`). Names are capped at 17 characters to fit the deck's column layout.

### Agent deck (`prefix+e`)

An fzf-based popup listing all panes (local and remote) with type, status, CPU, and memory. Sorted alphabetically by session with owner-based grouping. Repeated session and agent names are dimmed for readability.

Columns: **Pane** | **Type** | **Status** | **CPU** | **MEM**

- **Pane**: session name, with window/pane index for multi-pane sessions
- **Type**: icon + agent name (`🤖 claude`, `⚙ daemon`, `$` shell)
- **Status**: merged from `@pilot-status` (if set by external tools) or output-age heuristic
- **CPU/MEM**: summed across the entire process tree per pane

Orchestrator panes are marked with `★`, peer orchestrators with `★⇄`. Panes owned by an orchestrator are grouped under that orchestrator's section. Remote panes (fetched via SSH) appear in a separate host section.

Example:

```
PANE                  TYPE           ST  CPU   MEM
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
api-server            🤖 claude      ▶   5%  1.2G
frontend              🤖 vibe        ·   0%  236M
shell                  $                 0%   62M

── my-orch (2 agents) ────────────────────────
my-orch           ★   🤖 claude      ▶   1%  800M
my-orch.1              $             ▶   0%   90M
task-42               🤖 gemini      ⧖  45%  512M
task-99               🤖 vibe        !  23%  348M

── server01 ──────────────────────────────────
ci-runner@server01    🤖 gemini      ⧖
worker@server01       🤖 vibe        !
```

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `Enter` | Attach to pane (SSH for remote) |
| `Ctrl+R` | Refresh preview |
| `Ctrl+E` / `Ctrl+Y` | Scroll preview (line) |
| `Ctrl+D` / `Ctrl+U` | Scroll preview (half-page) |
| `Ctrl+W` | Toggle line wrap in preview |
| `Alt+D` | Git diff popup |
| `Alt+S` | Commit + push worktree |
| `Alt+X` | Kill pane + cleanup worktree |
| `Alt+P` | Pause agent (sends `Escape`) |
| `Alt+R` | Resume agent (sends `resume`) |
| `Alt+N` | Launch new agent |
| `Alt+E` | Edit session description |
| `Alt+Y` | Approve (send Enter to pane) |
| `Alt+T` | Change pane type (shell/agent/daemon) |
| `Alt+U` | Copy pane UUID to clipboard |
| `Alt+L` | View log |
| `Esc` | Close deck |

The preview panel (right side, 60%) shows metadata:

- **SES/WIN/PANE/UUID** — session, window, pane index, pane ID, UUID
- **CMD** — running command with runtime (e.g. `vibe (Python)`), agent name if different
- **DESC** — task description (auto-set from prompt)
- **STATUS** — merged status with owner and tier
- **PID/CPU/MEM/UP** — process info
- **ISSUE/TRUST** — task metadata
- **HOST/MODE** — remote host and execution mode
- **WORKDIR/VCS** — working directory and git status

All fields are shown only when set — empty fields are hidden.

#### Remote hosts

Remote panes are read over SSH from the hosts listed in
`~/.config/tmux-pilot/hosts`. To keep `prefix+e` instant, the deck
paints from local panes first and fetches remote panes
asynchronously: fzf shows the local list immediately, then swaps in
the full list (local + remote) as soon as the remote fetch returns.

Each remote fetch is bounded and runs in parallel, so a slow or
unreachable host can never freeze the deck. The overall per-host
timeout defaults to 3 seconds and can be tuned with the
`PILOT_SSH_TIMEOUT` environment variable. Hosts fetched in a
session are cached for the deck's lifetime so they don't flicker
out when the list is rebuilt after an action.

Manual check: add an unreachable host and confirm `prefix+e` still
opens instantly.

```bash
echo "192.0.2.1" >> ~/.config/tmux-pilot/hosts   # TEST-NET-1, black hole
# Open the deck with prefix+e — it appears immediately; the
# unreachable host simply contributes no panes.
sed -i '/^192\.0\.2\.1$/d' ~/.config/tmux-pilot/hosts   # clean up
```

### VCS status (`prefix+d`)

Opens neovim in a popup with:

- **Git repos**: `:Git` (vim-fugitive) — stage, diff, commit, blame
- **Mercurial repos**: `:Hgstatus` (vim-lawrencium)
- **Neither**: shows a message and waits for a keypress

Reads the `@pilot-workdir` pane variable first (set by agent hooks), falling back to `pane_current_path`. This ensures the popup opens in the repo the agent is actually working in, not just where it was launched.

### With [TPM](https://github.com/tmux-plugins/tpm)

```tmux
set -g @plugin 'AlexBurdu/tmux-pilot'
```

### Manual

```bash
git clone https://github.com/AlexBurdu/tmux-pilot ~/.tmux/plugins/tmux-pilot
```

Add to your `tmux.conf`:

```tmux
run-shell ~/.tmux/plugins/tmux-pilot/pilot.tmux
```

### Development

Clone the repo anywhere and symlink it into TPM's plugin directory:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/AlexBurdu/tmux-pilot ~/projects/tmux-pilot
cd ~/projects/tmux-pilot
./dev-setup.sh
```

## Configuration

All options are set via tmux options in your `tmux.conf`. Defaults are shown below — you only need to add lines for values you want to change.

```tmux
# Keybindings
set -g @pilot-key-new "a"
set -g @pilot-key-deck "e"
set -g @pilot-key-vcs "d"

# Popup sizes
set -g @pilot-popup-new-width "40%"
set -g @pilot-popup-new-height "30%"
set -g @pilot-popup-deck-width "95%"
set -g @pilot-popup-deck-height "90%"
set -g @pilot-popup-vcs-width "95%"
set -g @pilot-popup-vcs-height "90%"

# Status icons: use BMP symbols instead of emojis
# (for terminals with poor emoji rendering)
set -g @pilot-status-ascii "1"
```

## Session descriptions

Each agent session can have a short description (the `@pilot-desc` pane variable) displayed in the deck preview header as **DESC**. When you launch an agent via `prefix+a`, the description is auto-set from the first 80 characters of your prompt.

You can edit descriptions from the deck with `Alt+E`, or set them manually on any pane:

```bash
tmux set-option -p @pilot-desc "migrate auth to Compose"
```

Only panes with a description show the DESC line — others are unaffected.

### Pane Variables

tmux-pilot uses pane-level variables for metadata.
External tools can set additional variables that
tmux-pilot will display in the deck.

| Variable | Set by | Read by | Values |
|----------|--------|---------|--------|
| `@pilot-uuid` | pilot.tmux (auto) | deck, spawn | Unique pane identifier (12-char hex) |
| `@pilot-agent` | spawn.sh, auto-detect | deck, monitor | claude, gemini, agy, vibe, ... |
| `@pilot-desc` | spawn.sh, agent | deck | Task description |
| `@pilot-workdir` | agent hook | deck, kill.sh | Current dir |
| `@pilot-status` | external tool, deck | deck | Status enum (see below) |
| `@pilot-type` | spawn.sh, Alt+T | deck | shell, agent, daemon |
| `@pilot-owner` | spawn.sh (MCP) | deck, watchdog | UUID of the orchestrator that owns this agent |
| `@pilot-issue` | spawn.sh (MCP) | deck | Issue number |
| `@pilot-tier` | spawn.sh (MCP) | deck | Tier label |
| `@pilot-trust` | spawn.sh (MCP) | deck | Trust level |
| `@pilot-needs-help` | external tool | deck | "" or description |
| `@pilot-review-target` | orchestrator | external tool | Pane target for reviews |
| `@pilot-review-context` | orchestrator | external tool | Task-specific review hints |
| `@pilot-worktree` | spawn.sh (MCP) | deck | Worktree path |
| `@pilot-repo` | spawn.sh (MCP) | deck | Repo root path |

`@pilot-uuid` is assigned automatically to every pane on tmux startup and when new panes are created. It provides a stable identity that survives pane reordering (unlike `%NNN` pane IDs which tmux can reassign).

### Status enum

`@pilot-status` accepts a fixed set of values. The deck renders each as an emoji icon in the list and shows the raw value in the preview panel.

| Value | Icon | Meaning |
|-------|------|---------|
| `working` | `▶` | Agent is actively running |
| `watching` | `▶` | Being monitored |
| `waiting` | `!` | Needs human attention |
| `paused` | `‖` | Suspended (via pause) |
| `done` | `✓` | Task completed |
| `stuck` | `!` | Agent is stuck |
| *(empty)* | `·` | Idle, or derived from output age |

When `@pilot-status` is not set, the deck uses a heuristic based on the pane's last output time: recent output (`< 60s`) shows `▶`, older shows `·`. This ensures meaningful status for panes not managed by external tools.

External tools (monitoring daemons, orchestrators) write `@pilot-status` to communicate agent state. The deck sets it on pause (`paused`) and resume (`working`).

When `@pilot-needs-help` is set, `!` is shown regardless of `@pilot-status`.

```bash
# Examples
tmux set-option -p @pilot-status "working"
tmux set-option -p @pilot-status "waiting"
tmux set-option -p @pilot-needs-help "high-risk: rm -rf /"
```

### Review target

`@pilot-review-target` is an optional pane variable for routing review notifications. When set on an orchestrator pane, monitoring tools can route review-related events directly to this target instead of the orchestrator. This avoids consuming orchestrator context for review relay.

```bash
# Set on the orchestrator pane after spawning a review agent
tmux set-option -p @pilot-review-target "my-reviewer:0.0"
```

### Review context

`@pilot-review-context` is an optional pane variable for attaching task-specific review hints to a worker pane. When monitoring tools route review notifications to a review target, they can read this variable from the source pane and include it in the notification. This makes the review agent stateless — it receives fresh context with each event.

```bash
# Set on the worker pane after spawning
tmux set-option -p -t <worker-pane> @pilot-review-context "verify threshold stays at 10"
```

tmux-pilot does not read these variables itself — they are conventions for external monitoring tools that route events between panes.

## Working directory tracking

AI agents don't change their process's working directory, so tmux's `pane_current_path` stays at the launch directory even when the agent writes files elsewhere. tmux-pilot reads a pane-level variable `@pilot-workdir` to find the actual working directory.

To enable automatic tracking, add a PostToolUse hook to your agent's config. The hook fires after every file write/edit and stores the file's directory in the tmux pane variable.

### Claude Code

Add to `~/.claude/settings.json` (merge with existing hooks):

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [{
          "type": "command",
          "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty' | while IFS= read -r f; do [ -n \"$f\" ] && tmux set-option -p @pilot-workdir \"$(dirname \"$f\")\" 2>/dev/null; done; true"
        }]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Gemini CLI

Add to `~/.gemini/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "AfterTool": [
      {
        "matcher": "write_file|edit_file",
        "hooks": [{
          "type": "command",
          "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty' | while IFS= read -r f; do [ -n \"$f\" ] && tmux set-option -p @pilot-workdir \"$(dirname \"$f\")\" 2>/dev/null; done; true"
        }]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

> **Note**: The Gemini CLI hook reads `tool_input` from stdin as JSON. The exact field name may vary — use a debug hook (`cat > /tmp/gemini-hook-debug.json`) to confirm the schema.

## MCP Server

The MCP server lets any MCP-capable client (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, etc.) spawn and manage sibling agents programmatically — no interactive tmux popups needed.

This is also useful when developing tmux-pilot itself: an AI agent with the MCP server registered can spawn test sessions, inspect their state with `list_agents`, and clean them up — all without leaving the conversation.

### Install fastmcp

**macOS (Homebrew):**

```bash
brew install fastmcp
```

**Linux (pip):**

```bash
pip install fastmcp
```

Or with [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io/) to avoid polluting your system Python:

```bash
pipx install fastmcp
```

### Registration

Register the server with your MCP client using the CLI or by editing the config file directly.

Adjust the path below if you installed tmux-pilot elsewhere.

**Claude Code:**

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user tmux-pilot -- \
  python3 ~/.tmux/plugins/tmux-pilot/mcp/server.py
```

Or add to `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tmux-pilot": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["~/.tmux/plugins/tmux-pilot/mcp/server.py"]
    }
  }
}
```

**Gemini CLI:**

```bash
gemini mcp add tmux-pilot -- \
  python3 ~/.tmux/plugins/tmux-pilot/mcp/server.py
```

Or add to `~/.gemini/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tmux-pilot": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["~/.tmux/plugins/tmux-pilot/mcp/server.py"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Tools

| Tool | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `spawn_agent` | Create a new agent tmux session (agent, prompt, directory, optional session name) |
| `list_agents` | List all running panes with agent, owner, description, directory, age, CPU, memory |
| `pause_agent` | Gracefully pause a running agent (keeps pane alive for resume) |
| `resume_agent` | Resume a previously paused agent |
| `kill_agent` | Kill an agent session and clean up its worktree |
| `capture_pane` | Capture terminal text from a pane (target, optional line count) |
| `send_keys` | Send text or control keys to a pane (uses paste-buffer for text to bypass popups) |
| `monitor_agents` | Monitor all agent panes for permission prompts (risk-classified) and lifecycle events |
| `transfer_ownership` | Update @pilot-owner on all panes matching an old owner value (orchestrator handoff) |
| `run_command_silent` | Run a command silently, return exit code and tail of output (full output saved to log file) |

Title: fix(tmux): scope health authentication to trusted listeners
URL: https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/6158
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
# fix(tmux): scope health authentication to trusted listeners
...
- Remove the in-process server marker so tmux visualization always verifies the external OpenCode listener.
- Keep `tmux-core` harness-neutral through a lazy server-access capability; keep OpenCode provenance and Basic authentication in the adapter.
- Authenticate only a verified current-context listener or a listener selected by a valid explicit `OPENCODE_PORT`.
- Probe synthetic, raw, and historical addresses anonymously, and explicitly clear inherited OpenCode credentials on every OpenCode pane lifecycle path targeting them.
...
- Key successful health caching by normalized URL and an opaque request-policy identity, including redirect mode and credential changes.
- Reject an in-flight health result as soon as a different URL or request policy supersedes it, before it can authorize a tmux mutation or retry.
...
- Preserve historical panes after any direct HTTP response (including 401 or redirect); close only after two anonymous transport failures.
...
The active-listener readiness check calls `/global/health`, rejects redirects, and requires a successful response. Credential values are resolved lazily and are never stored in cache state or logs. Newly spawned or respawned panes for a verified listener receive the current credentials; panes for unverified addresses receive explicit empty credential variables. Existing panes and tmux's global environment are not rewritten.
...
Concurrent checks share authority by semantic identity: normalized health URL plus the HMAC identity of headers and redirect policy. A superseded request cannot retry, publish a cached success, or return `true`. Concurrent requests with the same policy, including an A-B-A transition back to an equivalent A policy, remain interchangeable.
...
Historical cleanup accepts only loopback HTTP(S) metadata without userinfo or port zero. Its probe uses `credentials: "omit"` and `redirect: "manual"`, so it neither forwards authentication nor contacts redirect targets.
...
- Real isolated OpenCode/private-tmux harness: 191/191 checks, including 30/30 explicit credential-clearing argv proofs across five untrusted provenances and six lifecycle surfaces; live DB count unchanged; no residual process, port, socket, or runtime directory.
...
The change is intentionally conservative: the canonical SDK default is anonymous unless explicit provenance identifies it. Listener or tmux failure still disables only visualization; agents and teams continue. No dependency or generated runtime artifact is changed.
...
A distinct pre-existing TOCTOU remains possible if the environment changes after a still-current health check returns and no competing check supersedes its policy. Eliminating that case would require a broader health-plus-environment lease API and is outside this targeted fix.
...

Title: iso/packages/iso-harness at main · Agent-Pattern-Labs/iso · GitHub
URL: https://github.com/Agent-Pattern-Labs/iso/tree/main/packages/iso-harness
Published: 2026-04-18T14:05:07.000Z
Author: Agent-Pattern-Labs
Highlights:
One config for every coding agent — Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi.
...
Keep your instructions, subagents, commands, and MCP servers in a single`iso/` directory.`iso-harness build` transpiles that source to the file layout each harness actually reads.
...
```
iso-harness build                         # reads ./iso, writes to ./
iso-harness build --target claude,cursor  # only two targets
iso-harness build --source path/to/iso --out path/to/project
iso-harness build --dry-run               # print planned writes, no disk changes
iso-harness build --watch                 # rebuild on every change under iso/
```
...
A harness-neutral schema. Each server has`command`, optional`args`, optional`env`. The emitter translates to the shape each harness expects (e.g. OpenCode wants`type: "local"` and`command` as an array).
...
By design,`mcp.json` has no per-harness override mechanism. The same MCP server should behave the same way no matter which harness launches it — if it doesn't, that's an MCP/config issue to fix at the server level, not something the shared config should paper over.
...
| Harness | Instructions | Agents | Commands | MCP |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `CLAUDE.md` | `.claude/agents/*.md` | `.claude/commands/*.md` | `.mcp.json` |
| Cursor | `.cursor/rules/main.mdc` | `.cursor/rules/agent-*.mdc` | (no native form) | `.cursor/mcp.json` |
| Codex | `AGENTS.md` | (no native form) | (no native form) | `.codex/config.toml` |
| OpenCode | `AGENTS.md` | `.opencode/agents/*.md` | `.opencode/skills/*.md` | `opencode.json` |
| Pi | `AGENTS.md` | `.pi/skills/*/SKILL.md` | `.pi/prompts/*.md` | (extension/package only) |
...
The abstraction is only as good as its lowest common denominator. Four explicit hatches keep harness-specific features possible:
...
1. Per-target frontmatter under`targets:`(agents & commands). Harness-specific fields under`targets. ` are mapped or passed through where that target supports them. Use this for OpenCode`temperature`/`fallback_models`, Claude Code`allowed-tools`, Pi skill metadata, etc.
2. `targets.: skip` omits the item from a specific target — useful when a subagent only makes sense in harnesses that support subagents.
3. `iso/config.json` with`targets.: { … }` for top-level harness config (not per-item). Keys under`targets.opencode` are merged into the generated`opencode.json`— use this for OpenCode's top-level`instructions: [...]` array, for example. Keys under`targets.pi` are merged into`.pi/settings.json`.
...
4. `iso/config.json` top-level`opencodeModelFallback`— JSON object written verbatim to`.opencode/opencode-model-fallback.json` for the@agent-pattern-labs/opencode-model-fallback plugin (`retryable_error_patterns`, global`fallback_models`, etc.). OpenCode-only; other harnesses ignore it.
...
`instructions.md` is still the shared base prompt. Optional sibling files let you add harness-specific root guidance without forking the whole source:
...
- `instructions.agents.md` appends only to the shared`AGENTS.md` output used by Codex, OpenCode, and Pi.
- `instructions.claude.md` appends only to`CLAUDE.md`.
- `instructions.cursor.md` appends only to`.cursor/rules/main.mdc`.
- `instructions.opencode.md` is emitted to`.opencode/instructions.md` and automatically added to`opencode.json.instructions`.
...
This is especially useful when OpenCode needs extra orchestration guidance that should not leak into the shared`AGENTS.md` file that Codex and Pi also read.
...
Per-agent OpenCode`fallback_models` still belong in agent frontmatter under`targets.opencode`. Use`opencodeModelFallback` only for the global plugin file OpenCode loads from`.opencode/`.
...
When@agent-pattern-labs/iso-route writes its resolved role map to` /.claude/iso-route.resolved.json`(normally by running`iso-route build` into the same output directory before`iso-harness build`), iso-harness picks it up automatically and stamps`model:` onto each Claude subagent frontmatter.

Yes. The closest exact match I found is [tmux-pilot](https://github.com/AlexBurdu/tmux-pilot).

It provides an fzf-based “agent deck” inside a tmux popup:

- Launches Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Aider, Goose, Open Interpreter, and other configurable agent CLIs.
- Discovers and controls ordinary tmux panes; agents remain their normal interactive processes.
- Supports switching, previewing output, sending approval, pausing/resuming, killing, viewing diffs, and launching another agent.
- Uses shell scripts, tmux metadata, and on-demand process inspection—no additional resident monitoring daemon is required for the palette.
- Its MCP server and agent-specific hooks are optional; the basic palette remains harness-neutral.

“Zero-daemon” here means zero daemon beyond tmux’s own server. That qualification applies to essentially every persistent tmux solution.

The catch: tmux-pilot is extremely new, has little adoption, and its README explicitly warns that it was vibe-coded. I would audit its pane-killing and worktree-cleanup scripts before trusting destructive shortcuts.

Nearby alternatives:

- [agentmux](https://github.com/Lockyc/agentmux) is also daemonless and lets TOML define essentially any CLI. It is a good lightweight launcher/session switcher, but it is less of a searchable command palette and richer status support currently depends on per-agent adapters.
- [ccmux](https://github.com/Yukaii/ccmux) has a considerably richer picker and multi-agent interface, but deliberately uses a background daemon.
- [llmux](https://github.com/cordfuse/llmux) is strongly harness-neutral and exposes CLI/REST/WebSocket control, but its architecture is explicitly daemon-based.
- [agent-tmux-manager](https://github.com/damellp/agent-tmux-manager) offers an advanced dashboard, layouts, prompt replies, and status tracking, but also requires `atmd`.
- For a minimal DIY version, [tmux](https://github.com/tmux/tmux) plus [fzf](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) is enough: enumerate panes with `tmux list-panes -a`, preview with `capture-pane`, select through `display-popup`/fzf, and act using `switch-client`, `send-keys`, or `kill-pane`.

results.stdout:
The short answer: I couldn’t find a public, end-to-end demo that combines all three characteristics—multi-floor racket-sports facility, operational digital twin, and autonomous building control. Public examples cover pieces of that stack.

### Closest public examples

| Project/demo | What it demonstrates | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| [Voltage Padel / Apollo3D case](https://www.ilkleygazette.co.uk/news/26247618.otley-firm-apollo3d-helping-drive-uk-padel-boom/) | Accurate CGI/360 model made from manufacturing information, used to test finishes and market the padel venue before construction finished | Closest racket-sports twin, but essentially a design/marketing twin rather than a live operational twin |
| [WWT digital twin of Energizer Park](https://www.wwt.com/video/wwt-digital-twin-st-louis-city-sc-energizer-park) | Public video of a BIM-derived Unreal Engine twin with 300,000+ controllable lights, VR/desktop interfaces, simulation, planning and venue operations | Strongest public operational sports-venue demo; not racket sports |
| [OnePlan’s Paris 2024 venue twins](https://www.oneplan.io/case-studies/paris-2024-olympics-digital-twins/) | Videos of browser-based twins used across 49 venues for security, workforce, transport, temporary infrastructure, accessibility and daily configurations | Strong operational-planning reference, including complex indoor venues; not autonomous building control |
| [LA Clippers / Intuit Dome VenueTwin](https://www.venuetwin.com/case-studies/la-clippers-venue-twin/) | Interactive multi-level arena visualization, suite and sight-line exploration, measurements, environmental scenarios and room configurations | Good reference for navigating a vertically complex facility, but mostly sales and planning |
| [Hightopo Virtual Stadium demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kqgYlSHVr0k) | 3D venue visualization combining crowd flow, energy use, equipment state and sensor data | Generic but visually close to an operational control-room twin |
| [Bosse Pickledom technology walkthrough](https://www.avnetwork.com/news/how-digital-projection-helped-deliver-a-show-stopping-video-wall-experience) | A real two-floor, 21-court pickleball complex with access control, lighting scenes, surveillance, networking and centralized AV | Excellent physical reference for a multi-floor racket venue—but no public digital twin appears to exist |

### Autonomous racket-facility references

These are operational automation products rather than spatial digital twins:

- [Doinsport autonomous padel/tennis courts](https://doinsport.com/en/autonomous-padel-tennis-courts): booking, payment, temporary QR/code access, remote unlocking and booking-synchronized lighting.
- [24x7Padel integrations](https://www.24x7padel.nl/en-gb/integrations): connects booking platforms with gates, payments, memberships and real-time activity reporting for unmanned clubs.
- [Tenkraft](https://tenkraft.com/): tennis/padel access control, lighting automation and 24-hour operation.
- [GS Access](https://gestion-sports.fr/systeme-acces-autonome/): reservation-linked door codes and lighting, with 4G and battery backup.
- [BOOQR padel facility software](https://www.booqr.software/en/padel-court-booking-system): booking, QR access, automatic lighting, payments, IoT integration and multi-court management.

The autonomous products generally provide dashboards, calendars and device status—but not a navigable floor-by-floor 3D twin.

### Open-source foundations for building the missing demo

A credible prototype could combine:

- [OpenRemote](https://github.com/openremote/openremote) for devices, MQTT/HTTP integrations, access state, energy, rules and dashboards. It includes a public demo and Docker quick-start.
- [xeokit BIM Viewer](https://github.com/xeokit/xeokit-bim-viewer) for browser-based IFC/BIM visualization, floor isolation and asset selection.
- [demoConstruct](https://singaporetech.github.io/immersification-demoConstruct/) for an open-source 3D twin whose reconstructed environment can receive incremental updates.
- Optionally, [CONTEXUS](https://contexus.io/) for a broader open-source BIM/IoT/building-management stack.

A compelling public demonstrator would model something like Bosse Pickledom, then animate court occupancy, reservations, access events, lighting, HVAC/energy, cleaning tasks and alarms across both floors. That exact combination appears to be an open niche rather than an already-polished public demo.

The most developed use case within sport is stadium and event management. Others are highly visual, data-driven 3D recreations of stadiums and the surrounding areas.
...
OnePlan’s virtual twin and geographic information software (GIS) mapping tools create digital venues that reflect the dimensions and capacity of a specific venue. They can be viewed at any angle, in any light, or in any weather condition, allowing users to see how changes to the venue impact lighting and audio quality, and determine where infrastructure such as barriers, fencing, vehicles, teams and volunteers should be placed.
...
OnePlan’s digital twins bring together multiple data sources, such as satellite imagery, drone footage, architectural drawings, transportation planning systems, and even the specifications of plastic seats. The detail of the final product, and the time it takes to create it, is dependent on the volume, quality, and format of available information.
...
Newer stadiums which have more structured, standardised datasets can be recreated in a matter of weeks, but older or data-poor venues can take much longer. ...

...
. Every four years, a single city must cope with an influx of millions of athletes, fans, administrators and media whilst also staging multiple championships at a vast array of venues.

For Paris, OnePlan built digital twins for every competition venue, allowing organisers to create detailed plans years in advance. This was especially important given the heavy reliance on existing or temporary venues, meaning organisers gained access very late or had no reference point to follow.
...
The digital twins also reduced the need for site visits by national Olympic committees (NOCs), international federations and individual teams, saving time and money and aiding the International Olympic Committee’s (IOC) sustainability initiatives. ...

...
Working with its technology partner NTT, the Tour combines topography and mapping information with real-time data extracted from sensors located along the route, underneath bike seats, and in support vehicles to gain visibility over key locations, assets and riders, making it easier to manage an event that is constantly moving – often in remote locations.
...

### Autonomous racket-facility references

These are operational automation products rather than spatial digital twins:

- [BOOQR padel facility software](https://www.booqr.software/en/padel-court-booking-system): booking, QR access, automatic lighting, payments, IoT integration and multi-court management.

The autonomous products generally provide dashboards, calendars and device status—but not a navigable floor-by-floor 3D twin.

### Open-source foundations for building the missing demo

A credible prototype could combine:

- [OpenRemote](https://github.com/openremote/openremote) for devices, MQTT/HTTP integrations, access state, energy, rules and dashboards. It includes a public demo and Docker quick-start.
- [xeokit BIM Viewer](https://github.com/xeokit/xeokit-bim-viewer) for browser-based IFC/BIM visualization, floor isolation and asset selection.
- [demoConstruct](https://singaporetech.github.io/immersification-demoConstruct/) for an open-source 3D twin whose reconstructed environment can receive incremental updates.
- Optionally, [CONTEXUS](https://contexus.io/) for a broader open-source BIM/IoT/building-management stack.

A compelling public demonstrator would model something like Bosse Pickledom, then animate court occupancy, reservations, access events, lighting, HVAC/energy, cleaning tasks and alarms across both floors. That exact combination appears to be an open niche rather than an already-polished public demo.

results.stdout:
The closest exact match is [TUR](https://github.com/aestriplex/tur), a niche open-source multi-repository commit tracker. It:

- Filters commits by one or more author/co-author email addresses.
- Takes an explicit list of repositories, so empty “bookmark forks” never appear.
- Outputs HTML or Jekyll/Markdown.
- Can group by repository, sort chronologically, and include commit messages/diff statistics.

Publish its generated Markdown or HTML through [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages) for a genuinely static public build log. This is the best fit for “work I authored,” rather than repositories I starred, forked, or merely own.

Useful references and alternatives:

- [TUR](https://github.com/aestriplex/tur) — strongest match; self-hosted static output and author-email filtering.
- [Duda & Nick’s Build Log](https://www.nicktimms.com/build-log) — a polished public example generated from GitHub commits, grouped by coder and product. Its generator does not appear to be publicly packaged.
- [BuilderLog](https://github.com/shubGupta10/builder-Log) and its [hosted app](https://builder-log-app.vercel.app/) — open source and produces public developer timelines, but it is a database-backed application and mixes commits with PRs and other activity, so it is not an exact static/authored-commits-only match.
- [git-standup](https://github.com/kamranahmedse/git-standup) — extracts your commits across local repositories and can produce a report, but you would need to add static-site formatting and publication yourself.
- [gshr](https://github.com/vogtb/gshr) — generates static browsable repository and commit-log pages, although it is repo-centric rather than specifically author-centric.

One important distinction: filtering repositories by GitHub ownership is insufficient. A useful build log should select commits by `author.email`/co-author identity, then group those commits by their originating repository. TUR follows that model and lets the repository list exclude passive forks explicitly. GitHub’s own [contribution activity](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/contribution-settings/viewing-contributions-on-your-profile) is not equivalent—it includes other contribution types and is neither a standalone static log nor a clean authored-commit export.
