# TUR - Multi-Repository Commit Tracker

TUR is an open-source command-line utility designed to help developers and project managers track commit histories across multiple repositories. By providing a flexible and feature-rich tool, TUR enables users to analyze and visualize commit contributions with ease.

## Features

* Track commits by one or multiple email addresses
* Support for multiple repositories via a simple repository list file
* Incremental cache: only newer commits are fetched when cache is enabled
* Interactive favorites/selection editing via a dedicated index file
* Multiple output formats:
    - Standard output (stdout)
    - LaTeX
    - HTML
    - Jekyll/Markdown
* Sorting and grouping options

## Requirements

* Make
* GCC (or compatible C compiler)
* libgit2

## Build

[![C/C++ CI](https://github.com/aestriplex/tur/actions/workflows/c-cpp.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/aestriplex/tur/actions/workflows/c-cpp.yml)

By simply running
```bash
make
```
You both build the tool and execute the tests. If you want to perform these operations separately, run
```bash
make tur
make test
```
To install just type
```bash
sudo make install
```
> **!** It's going to install tur in `/usr/local/bin`, so ensure to have it in your path.

## Usage

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help message |
| `-d`, `--diffs` | Shows the commit stats (line added, removed and file changed) |
| `-g`, `--group` | Group commits by repository |
| `-m, --message` | Shows the first line of the commit message |
| `-v`, `--version` | Display version |
| `--date-only` | Each commit will be printed without time information |
| `--no-ansi` | Avoid ANSI escape characters in terminal (e.g. colors) |
| `--no-cache` | Disable cache usage for the current run |
| `--clear-cache` | Remove all TUR cache files from `.tur/` |
| `-i`, `--interactive` | Open editor to select commits in `.tur/commits_index` |
| `-f`, `--force` | Recreate `.tur/commits_index` before interactive editing |
| `-e <e_1,...,e_n>`, `--emails <e_1,...,e_n>` | Provide a comma-separated list of emails |
| `-o <FILE>`, `--out <FILE>` | Specify an output file format (e.g., `.tex`, `.html`, `.md`) |
| `-r <FILE>`, `--repos <FILE>` | Specify a file containing repository paths |
| `-s`, `--sort` | Sort commits by date. You have to specify an order: ASC (Ascending order) or DESC (Descending order) |

Option `e` is required. If you don't specify any output file, it prints in `stdout`.

#### Cache files

When cache is enabled (default), TUR writes files in `.tur/`:

- `.tur/commits_cache`: full per-repository commit cache used for incremental loading
- `.tur/commits_index`: selected commits used for output and interactive edits

With cache enabled, TUR loads cached data and retrieves only commits newer than the latest cached commit. The interactive file is intentionally separate from full cache data.

If you run with `--no-cache`, TUR skips cache files and reads commits directly from repositories for that run.

#### Repository list

By default, TUR looks for a file called `.rlist` in the current path. The file should have this format
```
/path/to/local/repo1[origin/repo1/url]
/path/to/local/repo2[origin/repo2/url]
``` 
If you’d like to rename that file (or put it in another directory), you should specify its path via the option `-r`

#### Example of usage

The following command produce a LaTeX file with the grouped commit list, sorted by date (descending), in which `example@provider.com` is either the main author or the co-author.
```
% tur -f repository_list.txt -e example@provider.com -o commits.tex -g -s DESC
```
To specify more email adrresses, you can still use the option `-e` with the *comma-separated* list of emails:
```
% tur -f repository_list.txt -e example1@provider1.com,example2@provider2.com -o commits.tex -g -s DESC
```
Then you can add additional options like `-m` (to print the commit message) and `-d` to print the commit diff
```
$ tur -f repository_list.txt -e example1@provider1.com,example2@provider2.com -o commits.tex -gdm -s DESC
```
> **NOTE** The stdout output generates only textual bytes, so it's "easily greppable". If you want to avoid ANSI escape codes, you just have to use the option --no-ansi

So, a pipeline could look like this
```
$ tur -f repository_list.txt -e example1@provider1.com,example2@provider2.com -gdm -s DESC | grep repo1
```

#### Favorites in interactive mode

Run TUR with `-i` to open `.tur/commits_index` in your editor (from `GIT_EDITOR`, default: `vi`).
Mark a commit as favorite by adding `[*]` at the end of its line, then save and close the editor.

The closest exact match is [TUR](https://github.com/aestriplex/tur), a niche open-source multi-repository commit tracker. It:

- Filters commits by one or more author/co-author email addresses.
- Takes an explicit list of repositories, so empty “bookmark forks” never appear.
- Outputs HTML or Jekyll/Markdown.
- Can group by repository, sort chronologically, and include commit messages/diff statistics.

Publish its generated Markdown or HTML through [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages) for a genuinely static public build log. This is the best fit for “work I authored,” rather than repositories I starred, forked, or merely own.

Useful references and alternatives:

- [TUR](https://github.com/aestriplex/tur) — strongest match; self-hosted static output and author-email filtering.
- [Duda & Nick’s Build Log](https://www.nicktimms.com/build-log) — a polished public example generated from GitHub commits, grouped by coder and product. Its generator does not appear to be publicly packaged.
- [BuilderLog](https://github.com/shubGupta10/builder-Log) and its [hosted app](https://builder-log-app.vercel.app/) — open source and produces public developer timelines, but it is a database-backed application and mixes commits with PRs and other activity, so it is not an exact static/authored-commits-only match.
- [git-standup](https://github.com/kamranahmedse/git-standup) — extracts your commits across local repositories and can produce a report, but you would need to add static-site formatting and publication yourself.
- [gshr](https://github.com/vogtb/gshr) — generates static browsable repository and commit-log pages, although it is repo-centric rather than specifically author-centric.

One important distinction: filtering repositories by GitHub ownership is insufficient. A useful build log should select commits by `author.email`/co-author identity, then group those commits by their originating repository. TUR follows that model and lets the repository list exclude passive forks explicitly. GitHub’s own [contribution activity](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/contribution-settings/viewing-contributions-on-your-profile) is not equivalent—it includes other contribution types and is neither a standalone static log nor a clean authored-commit export.

results.stdout:
Yes—this pattern exists, although “JSON project manifest” has no widely adopted schema yet. The best public examples I found are:

- [Prasad Gade](https://prasadgade.dev/) — unusually comprehensive agent-ready developer portfolio. Publishes [`llms.txt`](https://prasadgade.dev/llms.txt) and [`api/projects.json`](https://prasadgade.dev/api/projects.json), alongside structured résumé, skills, social, OpenAPI, and agent-discovery documents.

- [Doug Finke](https://dougfinke.dev/) — AI tooling and automation portfolio. Publishes a concise [`llms.txt`](https://dougfinke.dev/llms.txt) and a first-class [`projects.json`](https://dougfinke.dev/projects.json) containing identity and project metadata.

- [Eduardo Urias](https://www.eduardourias.com/) — systems architect and AI-native product builder. Publishes [`llms.txt`](https://www.eduardourias.com/llms.txt) and [`api/projects.json`](https://www.eduardourias.com/api/projects.json); the latter includes fields such as project name, slug, type, status, and summary.

- [Keke Lebaka](https://kekelebaka.com/) — personal builder/operator site organized around several connected ventures. Publishes [`llms.txt`](https://kekelebaka.com/llms.txt) and [`projects.json`](https://kekelebaka.com/projects.json), plus an [`ai.json`](https://kekelebaka.com/ai.json) profile and a public evidence ledger.

- [Daliso Ngoma](https://daliso.com/) — founder and technology portfolio. Publishes [`llms.txt`](https://daliso.com/llms.txt) and a Schema.org-shaped [`api/projects.json`](https://daliso.com/api/projects.json). The implementation is open source in [DJNgoma/daliso-website](https://github.com/DJNgoma/daliso-website), and Daliso documents the agent-readiness work in [this implementation write-up](https://daliso.com/blog/how-we-got-from-23-to-92-on-is-your-site-agent-ready/).

A related agency/lab example is [MOZG](https://mozg.com.br/), which publishes [`llms.txt`](https://mozg.com.br/llms.txt) and a detailed [`data/site-projects.json`](https://mozg.com.br/data/site-projects.json), along with portfolio, capabilities, stacks, audit, and discovery exports documented on its [public API page](https://mozg.com.br/api).

My strongest references for an individual developer portfolio would be Prasad Gade for breadth, Doug Finke for simplicity, and Daliso Ngoma for an open-source, well-documented implementation. The recurring convention is:

```text
/llms.txt
/projects.json          or /api/projects.json
```

But field names and envelopes vary considerably; JSON Schema or a stable `version` field would make these manifests substantially more interoperable.

Publishes [`llms.txt`](https://prasadgade.dev/llms.txt) and [`api/projects.json`](https://prasadgade.dev/api/projects.json), alongside structured résumé, skills, social, OpenAPI, and agent-discovery documents.

- [Doug Finke](https://dougfinke.dev/) — AI tooling and automation portfolio. Publishes a concise [`llms.txt`](https://dougfinke.dev/llms.txt) and a first-class [`projects.json`](https://dougfinke.dev/projects.json) containing identity and project metadata.

- [Eduardo Urias](https://www.eduardourias.com/) — systems architect and AI-native product builder. Publishes [`llms.txt`](https://www.eduardourias.com/llms.txt) and [`api/projects.json`](https://www.eduardourias.com/api/projects.json); the latter includes fields such as project name, slug, type, status, and summary.

- [Keke Lebaka](https://kekelebaka.com/) — personal builder/operator site organized around several connected ventures. Publishes [`llms.txt`](https://kekelebaka.com/llms.txt) and [`projects.json`](https://kekelebaka.com/projects.json), plus an [`ai.json`](https://kekelebaka.com/ai.json) profile and a public evidence ledger.

- [Daliso Ngoma](https://daliso.com/) — founder and technology portfolio. Publishes [`llms.txt`](https://daliso.com/llms.txt) and a Schema.org-shaped [`api/projects.json`](https://daliso.com/api/projects.json). The implementation is open source in [DJNgoma/daliso-website](https://github.com/DJNgoma/daliso-website), and Daliso documents the agent-readiness work in [this implementation write-up](https://daliso.com/blog/how-we-got-from-23-to-92-on-is-your-site-agent-ready/).

A related agency/lab example is [MOZG](https://mozg.com.br/), which publishes [`llms.txt`](https://mozg.com.br/llms.txt) and a detailed [`data/site-projects.json`](https://mozg.com.br/data/site-projects.json), along with portfolio, capabilities, stacks, audit, and discovery exports documented on its [public API page](https://mozg.com.br/api).

My strongest references for an individual developer portfolio would be Prasad Gade for breadth, Doug Finke for simplicity, and Daliso Ngoma for an open-source, well-documented implementation. The recurring convention is:

```text
/llms.txt
/projects.json          or /api/projects.json
```

But field names and envelopes vary considerably; JSON Schema or a stable `version` field would make these manifests substantially more interoperable.

results.stdout:
Yes. I’d assemble this as three loosely coupled layers rather than adopt one “AI engineering platform.”

### 1. Company issue graph

Use the issue tracker as the workflow system, but maintain the cross-company graph separately.

- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) — modern Jira/Linear-like source system with work-item relationships, REST APIs, and webhooks. Community Edition is AGPL-3.0.
- [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) — more mature alternative when dependencies, portfolios, timelines, and conventional project governance matter more than UI polish.
- [Apache AGE](https://github.com/apache/age) — my default graph store if the company already operates PostgreSQL. It adds openCypher graph queries without introducing an entirely separate database.
- [Graphiti](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti) — useful enrichment layer for temporal facts extracted from documents, conversations, and agent activity. It preserves validity windows and provenance. I would not make probabilistically extracted Graphiti facts the authoritative issue record.
- [GrimoireLab](https://github.com/chaoss/grimoirelab) — niche but relevant ingestion and analytics components for correlating repositories, issues, reviews, mailing lists, and contributors.
- [OpenMetadata](https://github.com/open-metadata/OpenMetadata) or [DataHub](https://github.com/datahub-project/datahub) — worth borrowing entity, lineage, ownership, and ingestion patterns from if the graph will include services and datasets.

A useful initial ontology is:

```text
Issue ─blocks/duplicates/implements→ Issue
Issue ─affects→ Service
Issue ─requested_by→ Customer
Issue ─implemented_by→ PullRequest
PullRequest ─changes→ Repository
Deployment ─contains→ Commit
Incident ─caused_by/related_to→ Deployment
Decision ─justifies/supersedes→ Issue | Service | Decision
AgentRun ─attempted/resolved/produced→ Issue | Artifact
Person | Team ─owns→ Service | Issue
```

Every edge should carry `source`, `observed_at`, `valid_from`, `valid_to`, and `confidence`. Deterministic webhook-derived edges should remain distinct from agent-inferred edges.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Treat the contract as several small standards, not a single proprietary harness manifest.

- [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/specification) for tool inputs, outputs, task envelopes, artifacts, and structured errors.
- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture) for agent-to-tool and agent-to-context boundaries. MCP tools support input and output schemas, making them suitable for typed company-graph operations.
- [A2A Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/) for remotely discoverable agents, stateful tasks, messages, and artifacts. Use it only across process or organizational boundaries; it is excessive for internal function calls.
- [CloudEvents](https://cloudevents.io/) for durable lifecycle events such as `run.started`, `tool.completed`, `approval.requested`, and `artifact.published`.
- [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/) for traces, logs, metrics, tool-call correlation, and model usage.
- [Open Policy Agent](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/) for permission decisions and approval policy.
- [CUE](https://cuelang.org/docs/) for validating and composing harness manifests when JSON Schema alone becomes awkward.
- [OCI Runtime Specification](https://github.com/opencontainers/runtime-spec) for reproducible sandbox/container boundaries.

For reference implementations:

- [Inspect AI](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai) has strong task, tool, sandbox, transcript, and evaluation abstractions, including an [agent bridge](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/agent-bridge.html).
- [OpenHands](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands) is useful for studying coding-agent runtime, event, tool, and sandbox boundaries.
- [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) provides a narrower, inspectable agent–computer interface.
- [Open Harness](https://github.com/MaxGfeller/open-harness) is a smaller project worth watching for cross-harness adapters.
- The emerging [Harness Protocol](https://harnessprotocol.io/) directly targets portable `harness.yaml` configuration, but I would treat it as experimental until governance, compatibility testing, and adoption are clearer.

The minimal durable contract should define:

```text
TaskSpec       immutable intent, inputs, limits, acceptance checks
RunSpec        agent/runtime/model/environment/policy versions
ToolContract   JSON-schema input/output plus side-effect classification
EventEnvelope  sequence, causation, correlation, actor, timestamps
ArtifactRef    content hash, media type, provenance, storage location
RunResult      terminal state, outputs, evidence, costs, failure taxonomy
```

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

Compose proven TUIs first; build a unified cockpit only where integration adds real value.

- [Zellij](https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij) — workspace shell with layouts and plugins.
- [lazygit](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit) — repository operations.
- [gh-dash](https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash) — GitHub PR, issue, and notification dashboard; it can map repositories to local checkout paths.
- [k9s](https://github.com/derailed/k9s) — runtime/Kubernetes pane.
- [Taskwarrior](https://github.com/GothenburgBitFactory/taskwarrior) — local, scriptable task cache and personal queue.
- [lnav](https://github.com/tstack/lnav) — structured log exploration.
- [VisiData](https://github.com/saulpw/visidata) — excellent ad hoc inspection of exported issue, run, cost, and trace tables.
- [tea-dash](https://github.com/gbarany/tea-dash) — niche `gh-dash`-style option for Forgejo/Gitea.
- [lazyjira](https://github.com/textfuel/lazyjira) — niche Jira-focused cockpit if Jira remains upstream.

For a purpose-built cockpit, choose [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea) in Go or [Ratatui](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui) in Rust. I would expose five views:

1. Issue graph and blockers.
2. Active/queued agent runs.
3. Approval and policy inbox.
4. Artifacts, diffs, tests, and deployments.
5. Traces, costs, failures, and retry controls.

My pragmatic starting stack would be **Plane → PostgreSQL/Apache AGE → MCP tools → CloudEvents/OpenTelemetry → Zellij with gh-dash, lazygit, and a small Bubble Tea agent-run pane**. Add Graphiti only for inferred temporal context, and A2A only when independently deployed agents genuinely need interoperability.

Yes. I’d assemble this as three loosely coupled layers rather than adopt one “AI engineering platform.”

### 1. Company issue graph

Use the issue tracker as the workflow system, but maintain the cross-company graph separately.

- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) — modern Jira/Linear-like source system with work-item relationships, REST APIs, and webhooks. Community Edition is AGPL-3.0.
- [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) — more mature alternative when dependencies, portfolios, timelines, and conventional project governance matter more than UI polish.
- [Apache AGE](https://github.com/apache/age) — my default graph store if the company already operates PostgreSQL. It adds openCypher graph queries without introducing an entirely separate database.
- [Graphiti](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti) — useful enrichment layer for temporal facts extracted from documents, conversations, and agent activity. It preserves validity windows and provenance. I would not make probabilistically extracted Graphiti facts the authoritative issue record.
- [GrimoireLab](https://github.com/chaoss/grimoirelab) — niche but relevant ingestion and analytics components for correlating repositories, issues, reviews, mailing lists, and contributors.
- [OpenMetadata](https://github.com/open-metadata/OpenMetadata) or [DataHub](https://github.com/datahub-project/datahub) — worth borrowing entity, lineage, ownership, and ingestion patterns from if the graph will include services and datasets.

A useful initial ontology is:

```text
Issue ─blocks/duplicates/implements→ Issue
Issue ─affects→ Service
Issue ─requested_by→ Customer
Issue ─implemented_by→ PullRequest
PullRequest ─changes→ Repository
Deployment ─contains→ Commit
Incident ─caused_by/related_to→ Deployment
Decision ─justifies/supersedes→ Issue | Service | Decision
AgentRun ─attempted/resolved/produced→ Issue | Artifact
Person | Team ─owns→ Service | Issue
```

Every edge should carry `source`, `observed_at`, `valid_from`, `valid_to`, and `confidence`. Deterministic webhook-derived edges should remain distinct from agent-inferred edges.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Treat the contract as several small standards, not a single proprietary harness manifest.

- [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/specification) for tool inputs, outputs, task envelopes, artifacts, and structured errors.
- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture) for agent-to-tool and agent-to-context boundaries. MCP tools support input and output schemas, making them suitable for typed company-graph operations.
- [A2A Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/) for remotely discoverable agents, stateful tasks, messages, and artifacts. Use it only across process or organizational boundaries; it is excessive for internal function calls.
- [CloudEvents](https://cloudevents.io/) for durable lifecycle events such as `run.started`, `tool.completed`, `approval.requested`, and `artifact.published`.
- [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/) for traces, logs, metrics, tool-call correlation, and model usage.
- [Open Policy Agent](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/) for permission decisions and approval policy.
- [CUE](https://cuelang.org/docs/) for validating and composing harness manifests when JSON Schema alone becomes awkward.
- [OCI Runtime Specification](https://github.com/opencontainers/runtime-spec) for reproducible sandbox/container boundaries.

For reference implementations:

- [Inspect AI](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai) has strong task, tool, sandbox, transcript, and evaluation abstractions, including an [agent bridge](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/agent-bridge.html).
- [OpenHands](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands) is useful for studying coding-agent runtime, event, tool, and sandbox boundaries.
- [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) provides a narrower, inspectable agent–computer interface.
- [Open Harness](https://github.com/MaxGfeller/open-harness) is a smaller project worth watching for cross-harness adapters.
- The emerging [Harness Protocol](https://harnessprotocol.io/) directly targets portable `harness.yaml` configuration, but I would treat it as experimental until governance, compatibility testing, and adoption are clearer.

The minimal durable contract should define:

```text
TaskSpec       immutable intent, inputs, limits, acceptance checks
RunSpec        agent/runtime/model/environment/policy versions
ToolContract   JSON-schema input/output plus side-effect classification
EventEnvelope  sequence, causation, correlation, actor, timestamps
ArtifactRef    content hash, media type, provenance, storage location
RunResult      terminal state, outputs, evidence, costs, failure taxonomy
```

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

Compose proven TUIs first; build a unified cockpit only where integration adds real value.

- [Zellij](https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij) — workspace shell with layouts and plugins.
- [lazygit](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit) — repository operations.
- [gh-dash](https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash) — GitHub PR, issue, and notification dashboard; it can map repositories to local checkout paths.
- [k9s](https://github.com/derailed/k9s) — runtime/Kubernetes pane.
- [Taskwarrior](https://github.com/GothenburgBitFactory/taskwarrior) — local, scriptable task cache and personal queue.
- [lnav](https://github.com/tstack/lnav) — structured log exploration.
- [VisiData](https://github.com/saulpw/visidata) — excellent ad hoc inspection of exported issue, run, cost, and trace tables.
- [tea-dash](https://github.com/gbarany/tea-dash) — niche `gh-dash`-style option for Forgejo/Gitea.
- [lazyjira](https://github.com/textfuel/lazyjira) — niche Jira-focused cockpit if Jira remains upstream.

For a purpose-built cockpit, choose [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea) in Go or [Ratatui](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui) in Rust. I would expose five views:

1. Issue graph and blockers.
2. Active/queued agent runs.
3. Approval and policy inbox.
4. Artifacts, diffs, tests, and deployments.
5. Traces, costs, failures, and retry controls.

My pragmatic starting stack would be **Plane → PostgreSQL/Apache AGE → MCP tools → CloudEvents/OpenTelemetry → Zellij with gh-dash, lazygit, and a small Bubble Tea agent-run pane**. Add Graphiti only for inferred temporal context, and A2A only when independently deployed agents genuinely need interoperability.

Company issue graph\n\nRecommended stack:\n\n- Plane as the human-facing issue/project system of record.\n - Issues, cycles, modules, views, triage, and API.\n - AGPL-3.0.\n - https://github.com/makeplane/plane\n - https://developers.plane.so/api-reference/introduction\n\n- PostgreSQL + Apache AGE as the authoritative graph projection.\n - AGE adds graph storage and Cypher queries to PostgreSQL, avoiding a second operational database.\n - Apache-2.0.\n - https://github.com/apache/age\n - https://age.apache.org/\n\n- Graphiti only for derived temporal/semantic memory.\n - Useful for extracting entities, decisions, and changing relationships from issue comments, run logs, and documents.\n - Do not make LLM-extracted Graphiti edges authoritative; retain provenance back to the original issue, commit, artifact, or message.\n - Apache-2.0.\n - https://github.com/getzep/graphiti\n - https://help.getzep.com/graphiti/getting-started/overview\n\nA practical graph model:\n\n```text\nCompany → Team → Project → Issue\nIssue → PR → Commit\nIssue → Run → Artifact\nIssue → Decision\nRun → Agent\n```\n\nTyped edges should include `BLOCKS`, `DUPLICATES`, `IMPLEMENTS`, `CAUSED_BY`, `SUPERSEDES`, `VERIFIED_BY`, and `PRODUCED`. Every derived edge should carry source URL, source revision, extractor version, confidence, and timestamp.\n\n2. Agent harness contracts\n\nUse small public standards at each boundary:\n\n- JSON Schema for your own stable `Task`, `Run`, `Event`, `Artifact`, `Evidence`, and `Review` objects.\n - https://json-schema.org/\n\n- CloudEvents as the event envelope.\n - Gives events standard IDs, source, type, subject, time, and content type.\n - https://cloudevents.io/\n - https://github.com/cloudevents/spec\n\n- MCP for agent-to-tool and agent-to-resource access.\n - Good for issue queries, repository operations, test runners, graph lookups, and artifact retrieval.\n - It is not a complete workflow or agent-to-agent protocol.\n - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest\n - https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/specification\n\n- A2A for remote agent discovery and agent-to-agent task exchange.\n - Use only when agents are independently deployed services; don’t require it for local subprocess workers.\n - Apache-2.0.\n - https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A\n\n- AGENTS.md for repository-local operating instructions.\n - https://agents.md/\n\n- Inspect for reproducible evaluation tasks, solvers, scorers, sandboxes, and logs.\n - Better suited to evaluations than production orchestration.\n - https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/\n - https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai\n\n- OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions for traces and metrics.\n - https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/tree/main/docs/gen-ai\n\nI would define the harness around an append-only event stream:\n\n```text\ntask.created\nrun.started\nagent.message\ntool.requested\ntool.completed\nartifact.produced\nevidence.attached\nreview.requested\nreview.resolved\nrun.completed\nrun.failed\n```\n\nThe critical contract is not the prompt. It is the immutable record connecting inputs, tool calls, code revision, artifacts, evidence, reviewer decisions, and final status.\n\n3. https://github.com/anomalyco/opentui\n - https://opentui.com/\n\n- Go: Bubble Tea\n - Mature Elm-style architecture with a strong component ecosystem.\n - MIT.\n - https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea\n\n- Python: Textual\n - Rich widgets, CSS-like styling, async operation, testing support, and terminal/web targets.\n - MIT.\n - https://github.com/Textualize/textual\n - https://textual.textualize.io/\n\nUseful public UX references:\n\n- Lazygit for pane navigation, contextual commands, and preview/detail transitions:\n https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit\n\n- k9s for live resource tables, drill-down, filtering, logs, command mode, and keyboard discoverability:\n https://github.com/derailed/k9s\n\nSuggested cockpit layout:\n\n```text\n┌ Projects / queues ┬ Issue or run graph ┬ Evidence / live output ┐\n│ assigned │ dependencies │ logs │\n│ blocked │ agents and runs │ diffs │\n│ awaiting review │ artifacts │ tests │\n│ recently failed │ provenance │ reviewer annotations │\n└───────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nRecommended default combination\n\n- Plane for issue authoring and collaboration\n- PostgreSQL + Apache AGE for the authoritative company graph\n- Graphiti for optional semantic/temporal enrichment\n- JSON Schema + CloudEvents for internal contracts\n- MCP for tools/resources\n- A2A only across independently deployed agent services\n- Inspect for evaluations\n- OpenTelemetry for observability\n- OpenTUI for a TypeScript terminal cockpit\n\nThat creates a replaceable architecture: the graph, harness, agents, and cockpit share contracts without any one agent framework owning the company’s operational data.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/bench-2026-07-31T10-05-34/raw.json:75: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/bench-2026-07-31T10-05-34/raw.json:84: "stdout": "Kevin Rajan, online as `kvnloo`, describes himself as a builder, engineer, scientist, solutions architect, systems thinker, and automation-orchestration specialist. But the API gives you the right primitive for \"authored only,\" so it's little work.\n\n## The primitive that does the filtering for you\n\n**GraphQL `contributionsCollection.commitContributionsByRepository`** — this is authored-commits-only by construction. Stars never appear (they live under a separate connection), and forks you merely bookmarked have zero commit contributions so they drop out automatically. Docs: https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#contributionscollection\n\n```graphql\nquery($login:String!, $from:DateTime!) {\n user(login:$login) {\n contributionsCollection(from:$from) {\n commitContributionsByRepository(maxRepositories:100) {\n repository { nameWithOwner url isFork isPrivate primaryLanguage { name } }\n contributions { totalCount }\n }\n }\n }\n}\n```\n\nCaveats worth knowing before you build on it: `from`/`to` must span ≤1 year, so you loop year by year; and commits only count if the author email is verified against the account (https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/setting-up-and-managing-your-personal-account-on-github/managing-contribution-settings-on-your-profile/why-are-my-contributions-not-showing-up-on-my-profile).\n\n## REST alternatives\n\n- Own repos: `GET /users/{u}/repos?type=owner` then drop `fork === true` — https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/repos#list-repositories-for-a-user\n- Per-repo authored commits: `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/commits?author={u}` — https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits#list-commits\n- Cross-repo: `GET /search/commits?q=author:{u}+sort:author-date` — https://docs.github.com/en/rest/search/search#search-commits (rate limit is 30/min authenticated; it also misses commits made under unlinked emails)\n- Avoid `GET /users/{u}/events/public` as the backbone — capped at 300 events / 90 days: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/activity/events\n\n## Existing projects you can crib or use directly\n\n- **lowlighter/metrics** — https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics — renders SVG panels from your contribution data via Actions. Very close to what you want in spirit; note the repo is no longer actively developed, so treat it as reference more than dependency.\n- **anuraghazra/github-readme-stats** — https://github.com/anuraghazra/github-readme-stats — hosted SVG cards; its `count_private`/commit-count logic is a useful read, though the default cards mix in stars.\n- **OSS Insight** — https://ossinsight.io/ — query GitHub archive data, including per-user authored-commit breakdowns, without running your own crawler.\n- **GH Archive** — https://www.gharchive.org/ — the raw event firehose, queryable from BigQuery, if you want a full historical log rather than API-window slices.\n\n## Recommended shape\n\nActions workflow on a `schedule:` cron → GraphQL loop over years → write `data/commits.json` → commit it → static page renders from that file. The committed JSON is what makes the log genuinely static and diffable, and it survives API outages. `GITHUB_TOKEN` in Actions covers the auth; scheduled workflows on public repos are free.\n\nGiven you already have `data/` and a runner pattern in this repo, that fits the existing structure — say the word and I'll wire it up against your username.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/bench-2026-07-31T10-06-27/raw.json:163: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/bench-2026-07-31T10-06-27/raw.json:172: "stdout": "I can't verify live — WebSearch permission isn't granted in this session, so nothing below is checked against the current state of those sites. Treating this as \"from public knowledge,\" with the caveat that per-site file presence changes often.\n\n**The honest answer: there is no established convention here.** `llms.txt` is a real, documented spec; a companion JSON project manifest is not. Nobody agreed on a schema, and no crawler consumes one. So the pattern you're describing is mostly individual experimentation rather than a practice with exemplars worth copying wholesale.\n\nWhat actually exists publicly:\n\n- **llms.txt spec** — Jeremy Howard's proposal, markdown index at `/llms.txt` plus optional expanded `/llms-full.txt`: https://llmstxt.org/ and https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt\n- **Directory of adopters** — https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/ and https://llmstxt.site/ list sites serving one. Both are dominated by docs sites (Anthropic, Zapier, Cloudflare, Perplexity, Mintlify-hosted docs) rather than personal portfolios. If you want real portfolio examples, these directories are the place to filter, not my recall.\n- **Mintlify auto-generation** — https://mintlify.com/docs/ai/llmstxt — why so much of the adoption is docs platforms flipping a switch.\n\nFor the JSON half, the parts that are actually standardized and machine-consumed today:\n\n- **schema.org `Person` + `CreativeWork`/`SoftwareSourceCode`** as JSON-LD in your HTML.               \\n./index.html:174:

              builder. engineer. scientist. solutions architect. systems thinker. automation orchestration expert. code is the great equalizer. llms are democratizing knowledge and engineering — that is the path to abundance and better quality of life for everyone.

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
results.stdout:
For most independent dental clinics in 2026, **RevenueWell is the best overall dental CRM**. It combines patient acquisition, recall/reactivation, reminders, two-way texting, forms, reviews, payments, and practice-management-system integration without requiring you to construct healthcare workflows in a generic CRM.

### Best options by use case

| Product | Best for | HIPAA-related evidence | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[RevenueWell](https://www.revenuewell.com/)** | Best overall for independent clinics | RevenueWell identifies itself as a business associate, documents encrypted data transfer and HIPAA/HITECH controls, and offers healthcare-specific communications. See its [HIPAA documentation](https://www.revenuewell.com/hipaa-compliance). | Confirm the BAA is incorporated into your particular contract and ask which modules it covers. |
| **[NexHealth](https://www.nexhealth.com/)** | Best patient-experience layer alongside Dentrix, Open Dental, Eaglesoft, etc. | HIPAA and SOC 2 controls, mandatory 2FA, audit logging, scheduling, forms, texting and payments. See its [compliance statement](https://help.nexhealth.com/en/articles/12754290-what-is-nexhealth-s-legal-and-security-compliance-status) and [Trust Center](https://security.nexhealth.com/). | It is primarily a front-office/engagement layer, not a full clinical PMS. Explicitly request and review the BAA. |
| **[Weave](https://www.getweave.com/)** | Best when phones, texting and payments should be consolidated | Weave publishes its actual [Business Associate Agreement](https://www.getweave.com/legal/baa/) and documents encryption, role-based access, MFA and audit-trail expectations in its [HIPAA software guide](https://www.getweave.com/hipaa-software-compliance/). | Strongest value depends on replacing or consolidating your phone system. Review its BAA provisions concerning internal analytics and AI use of PHI. |
| **[CareStack](https://carestack.com/)** | Best all-in-one for DSOs and multi-location groups | Combines CRM/patient engagement with clinical records, billing and centralized reporting. ### My practical recommendation

- **One or a few locations with an existing PMS:** choose **RevenueWell** for growth/recall or **NexHealth** for scheduling and front-desk automation.
- **Phone-heavy clinic:** choose **Weave**.
- **Growing DSO replacing several systems:** shortlist **CareStack**.

Self-hosting does not itself create HIPAA compliance.

### Non-negotiable purchasing checklist

Before transmitting any PHI:

1. Obtain a signed BAA covering every purchased module, integration and AI feature.
2. Require MFA, unique user accounts, role-based access and exportable audit logs.
3. Verify encryption at rest and in transit, backup recovery, retention/deletion and breach-notification terms.
4. Ask where call recordings, texts, forms and AI transcripts are stored and whether they train models.
5. Test the exact PMS integration using a sandbox or de-identified records.
6. Conduct your own security-risk analysis and staff training.

A vendor cannot simply “certify” your clinic as compliant. HHS says covered entities need written arrangements with business associates that protect PHI; the BAA and the clinic’s actual configuration and operations both matter. See the official [HHS Business Associate guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html).

There are two separate sets of regulations that govern the sharing of patient data: HIPAA (the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996), which establishes your practice as a “Covered Entity” and regulates how you use and disclose protected health information (PHI); and the HITECH Act (Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act of 2009), which complements HIPAA and controls with whom you can share this information. Parties with whom you share such information are identified as “Business Associates,” and must comply with HIPAA Privacy and Security rules to the same degree as any covered entity. In this framework, RevenueWell acts as your Business Associate, and your office is the Covered Entity.
...
The 2013 amendments to the HIPAA rules under the HITECH Act state a covered entity is required to obtain prior authorization from the patient to “market” to them, which is defined as “making a communication about a product or service that encourages recipients of the communication to purchase or use the product or service” [Title 45 of the Code of Federal Regulations, section 164.501].
...
However, HIPAA offers exemptions for communications about services you render or offer as their healthcare provider, as well as “healthcare operations” communications around treatment plans, alternatives to treatment, new services and care coordination. The only instance when such messages could be considered “marketing,” and would thus require permission from the recipient, would be if a Covered Entity or their Business Associate received third-party “financial remuneration” to send these messages. This isn’t common in a typical dental office – and RevenueWell as a business associate never accepts any form of third-party remuneration for content within the system.
...
- Email: Health care providers are permitted to communicate with their patients electronically (including email), as long as reasonable precautions and safeguards are taken to limit unintentional disclosure [45 C.F.R § 164.530(c)]. Because RevenueWell utilizes patient contact information directly from your practice management software, it is your responsibility to ensure that you have each patient’s correct email address on file.
...
- Phone Calls and Answering Machine Messages: A Covered Entity or a Business Associate may leave a message on an answering machine, with a family member, or with another person who answers the phone when the patient is not home, so long as a reasonable precaution is taken to limit the amount of information disclosed in such a non-personal interaction [45 C.F.R § 164.510(b)(3)]. RevenueWell’s phone calls (and answering machine messages) do not contain any treatment-specific information and hence comply with this requirement.
...
- Postcards and Letters: Business Associates are allowed to mail correspondence to a patient’s home or other specified mailing addresses on behalf of a Covered Entity even if it contains PHI. As an additional measure of security, RevenueWell uses covered envelopes for any correspondence containing health-related or payment-related information. Again, as with email addresses, your office needs to take the necessary precautions to ensure that the patient’s mailing address is listed correctly in the practice management software.

Data extracted from your practice management software is sent over an encrypted Internet connection to RevenueWell’s secure, HIPAA, HITECH and PCI-compliant hosting facility, where all data operations are performed. Telephone Consumer Protection Act rules are designed to protect consumers from telemarketing messages, and apply to text messaging, residential phone lines, and wireless lines. Review its BAA provisions concerning internal analytics and AI use of PHI. |
| **[CareStack](https://carestack.com/)** | Best all-in-one for DSOs and multi-location groups | Combines CRM/patient engagement with clinical records, billing and centralized reporting. CareStack states HIPAA compliance plus SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO 27001:2022 certification; see its [HIPAA dental-software page](https://carestack.com/dental-software/features/hipaa-compliant). | Larger implementation, data migration and organizational change than adding a CRM to an existing PMS. |
| **[HubSpot](https://www.hubspot.com/products/crm)** | Best customizable CRM for a sophisticated marketing team or large DSO | HubSpot supports HIPAA-covered data through Sensitive Data settings and an applicable BAA. Its documentation explains [how to enable HIPAA-covered data](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/account-security/store-sensitive-data) and identifies the [features covered for sensitive data](https://legal.hubspot.com/hubspot-product-and-services-catalog). | Enterprise-level cost and significant dental workflow/integration work. PHI is permitted only in covered features—not automatically everywhere in HubSpot. |

### My practical recommendation

- **One or a few locations with an existing PMS:** choose **RevenueWell** for growth/recall or **NexHealth** for scheduling and front-desk automation.
- **Phone-heavy clinic:** choose **Weave**.
- **Growing DSO replacing several systems:** shortlist **CareStack**.
- **Centralized corporate marketing across many brands:** consider **HubSpot Enterprise**, but only after mapping every PHI data flow to its Sensitive Data covered services.

I would not put patient data in a generic CRM—or a self-hosted open-source CRM such as [SuiteCRM](https://github.com/SuiteCRM/SuiteCRM)—unless the clinic is prepared to own encryption, logging, backups, patching, access controls, incident response, integrations and every relevant subcontractor agreement. Self-hosting does not itself create HIPAA compliance.

### Non-negotiable purchasing checklist

Before transmitting any PHI:

1. Obtain a signed BAA covering every purchased module, integration and AI feature.
2. Require MFA, unique user accounts, role-based access and exportable audit logs.
3. Verify encryption at rest and in transit, backup recovery, retention/deletion and breach-notification terms.
4. Ask where call recordings, texts, forms and AI transcripts are stored and whether they train models.
5. Test the exact PMS integration using a sandbox or de-identified records.
6. Conduct your own security-risk analysis and staff training.

A vendor cannot simply “certify” your clinic as compliant. HHS says covered entities need written arrangements with business associates that protect PHI; the BAA and the clinic’s actual configuration and operations both matter. See the official [HHS Business Associate guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html).

Try this 25-minute creamy mushroom and spinach pasta, adapted from [Good Food’s recipe](https://www.bbcgoodfood.com/recipes/creamy-mushroom-spinach-pasta).

**Serves 2**

- 6 oz / 170 g pasta
- 8 oz / 225 g mushrooms, sliced
- 3 packed cups baby spinach
- 2 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 small shallot or half an onion, diced
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- ½ cup crème fraîche, heavy cream, or cream cheese
- ¼ cup grated Parmesan
- Salt, black pepper, and optional red-pepper flakes

1. Boil the pasta in salted water. Reserve about ½ cup pasta water before draining.
2. Meanwhile, heat the oil in a large skillet. Cook the mushrooms and onion over medium-high heat for 7–9 minutes, until browned. Avoid stirring constantly—letting the mushrooms sit helps them color.
3. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds.
4. Lower the heat. Stir in the cream and Parmesan, followed by the spinach.
5. Add the drained pasta and a splash of pasta water. Toss until glossy and the spinach wilts, adding more water as needed.
6. Season generously with pepper, salt, and red-pepper flakes.

A squeeze of lemon at the end cuts through the richness nicely. For extra protein, add white beans, shredded chicken, or Italian sausage.

15 平台、多后端。**本 skill 存在时必须用它访问这些平台，不要自己发明方案。**

## 常驻规则（全程适用）

1. **动手前先体检**：多后端/登录态平台（小红书/Reddit/B站/Twitter/Facebook/Instagram）先跑
   `agent-reach doctor --json`，按各平台 `active_backend` 字段选命令组。
2. **声明你在用什么**：开始干活前说一句「使用 agent-reach 的 X 平台 / Y 后端」。
